HON. NICHOLAS LONGWORTH MESSAGE OF CONDOLENCE FROM SPEAKER ON DEATH OF LATE SPEAKER OF THE HOUSE OF REPRESENTATIVES
speechtext:
I have the honour to inform the house that during the Easter adjournment I sent the following telegram to the widow of the late Speaker of the House of Representatives of the United States:
Ottawa, April 10, 1931. Mrs. Nicholas Longworth,
Washington, D.C.
On behalf of the House of (.'ominous of Canada I tender you sincere sympathy on the passing of your husband whose record in the public life of his country merited the admiration of all.
George Black,
Speaker.

Privilege-Mr. Power
On the orders of the day:

I should like to ask the Minister of Marine whether he is aware that on the very day the house adjourned for the Easter recess many returned soldiers were dismissed from the Vancouver harbour board police force. If this is so, will he consider the reinstatement of these men?
I have no official knowledge of the fact referred to by my hon. friend. I will inquire and report.
On the orders of the day:

May I ask the Acting Minister of Labour a question based on two statements that appear in the Ottawa Journal this morning? On page two of the Ottawa Journal of April 13, I find this:
Montreal, April 12-Canadian Press dispatch. About one million people found employment under the joint federal, provincial, municipal relief fund last winter, declared Hon. Alfred Duranleau, K.C., Minister of Marine, addressing electors of Chambly-Vercheres county at a large sugaring party to-day.
Then I turn to page five of the same newspaper, and I read this:
The passing by parliament of the twenty million dollar unemployment relief fund in September last has resulted in employment being given to 248,274 persons, according to a statement issued by the Department of Labour covering the period to the end of March.
May I ask the Acting Minister of Labour which of the two statements is correct?

speakerposition: Minister of Immigration and Colonization; Minister of Mines
speechtext: I trust I am not responsible for what appears in the press.
Does the Minister of Marine deny the statement or is it true?

subtopic: REPORTED RETIREMENT OF EMPLOYEES OF DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR

speechtext: On the orders of the day:

subtopic: REPORTED RETIREMENT OF EMPLOYEES OF DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR
speechtext:
I should like to make this inquiry of the ministry through the Minister of the Interior:
First, is the newspaper report of Saturday true that there have been approximately one hundred positions of the Department of the Interior abolished?
Second, if so, is it the intention of the government to keep on the eligible list the civil
servants formerly occupying these positions and at the first opportunity to transfer them to positions in other departments for which they can qualify?

speakeroldname: Hon. T. G. MURPHY (Minister of the Interior):
speakerposition: Minister of the Interior; Superintendent-General of Indian Affairs
subtopic: REPORTED RETIREMENT OF EMPLOYEES OF DEPARTMENT OF THE INTERIOR
speechtext: The answer to the first question is in the affirmative. As to the second question, I can only say that the department are working in cooperation with the Civil Service Commission, who are cognizant of what is being done. As to what will be done in the future, that of course will depend upon a further conference with the Civil Service Commission.
On the orders of the day:

I
desire to draw the attention of Your Honour and of the house to a question of privilege. In an edition of a newspaper called Le Journal, published in Quebec city on the 4th April, there appears the following:
Le doeteur Duguay se signale par ses paroles opportunes.
That is to say:
Doctor Duguay, the member for Lake St. John, makes very opportune observations.
It goes further and says that the Benjamin of the house paints a soul-stirring picture of the history of Canadian politics, and so on through four columns of what purports to be a report of the speech by the hon. member for Lake St. John.
In Le Petit Journal, published in Montreal on the 5th of April, 1931, the following appears under the title of the Hon. Mr. Dupre, Solicitor General:
The speaker of the day on Thursday was the Hon. Maurice Dupre, minister of the district of Quebec. It was his parliamentary debut. He did very well. An eloquent speaker, a delicate litterateur, he examined the political situation and corrected the mistakes of the opposition.
He was loudly applauded by the right.
Go on with the question of privilege.

I would suggest that my
hon. friend do not talk too much or they will make a minister of him and keep him even quieter.
Referring to May's Parliamentary Practice, twelfth edition, page 75, I read:
The publication of the debates of either house has been repeatedly declared to be a breach of privilege, and especially false and perverted reports of them; and no doubt can exist that if either house desires to withhold
Privilege-Mr. Power

the proceedings from the public, it is within the strictest limits of their jurisdiction to do so, and to punish any violation of their orders.
Going back as far as 1641, it was ordered by the commons of England:
That no member shall either give a copy or publish in print anything that he shall speak here, without leave of the house; and that all the members of the house are enjoined to deliver out no copy or notes of anything that is brought into the house or that is propounded or agitated in the house.
This question of the publication of the debates has been discussed at great length, and through succeeding parliaments since parliaments have begun in Great Britain. At page 75 of May I find that the commons have permitted the publication of debates:
So long as the debates are correctly and faithfully reported the privilege which prohibits their publication is waived: but when they are reported mala fide,, the publishers of newspapers are liable to censure.
The point to which I wish to direct the attention of the house is this: I do not desire to make any reflection on the members who were inadvertently falsely reported, but I submit that the Speaker of the house, and particularly the Prime Minister in whose custody are the privileges of the house, should in some way call to the attention of these newspapers the breach of privilege which they have committed. I put the matter to the Prime Minister first because, as I have said, he is the guardian of the privileges of the House of Commons, and, secondly, because I suspect that he has perhaps given his blessing on more than one occasion to some of the newspapers. I also suggest very humbly that if the right hon. gentleman permitted his members to talk more often in the house they might not require to have recourse to publications in the newspapers. If it were the sense of the house I could make a motion that these articles be regarded as breaches of privilege.
I am satisfied however, if the house has no objection, to leave the matter in your hands, sir, and in those of the right hon. the Prime Minister.

I am afraid times have changed considerably since the year 1600 and to my knowledge within the past hundred years there have been thousands of such breaches of privilege. I do not condone them, but in this case I do not see that any particular harm has been done. I think the hon. member is wise to leave the matter as it is.

I am complaining not of
the publication of speeches but of a false report made of the proceedings of this house. I consider that a very serious matter. No speech was made; the hon. member (Mr. Duguay) made no speech, and neither did the hon. the Solicitor General.

Does the hon. member
suggest any harm has been done?
I suggest that to say something transpired in this house which as a matter of fact did not transpire constitutes a breach of privilege.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OP CANADA AT MEETING IN LONDON

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

subtopic: REPRESENTATION OP CANADA AT MEETING IN LONDON
speechtext:
In view of the fact that the date has
now been fixed for the wheat conference at London I would like to ask a question of the Prime Minister. Is the Hon. G. Howard Ferguson to be the only Canadian representative at that conference and if not is the right hon. Prime Minister in a position to state what the representation will be?

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
subtopic: REPRESENTATION OP CANADA AT MEETING IN LONDON
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, no report other than a
cabled report has yet been received. The chief statistician of the Dominion who has been absent in Rome is returning to Canada. When he arrives and when we receive by mail a despatch from the High Commissioner at London I will be in a better position to inform the hon. member.
On the orders of the day.

I would like to ask the Prime Minister who is acting for the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) whether a statement which appeared in this morning's paper is true. I have not the article before me but the effect of it was that shortly there would be introduced into this house a trade treaty with Australia. This is a very important matter and a rather unusual way to announce a government policy. No mention of such a treaty was made in the speech from the throne and such action by the government would greatly affect the province of British Columbia. I would like to ask if the statement as reported in the paper is true?

St. Lawrence Waterway

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
Once more perhaps the house realizes
that statements of intended policies of happenings frequently appear in newspapers. The newspapers using their best judgment have conjectured that many things may happen. The hon. gentleman will have to attach to such a statement such weight as he thinks proper. At the present time the government has no intention of discussing the matter.

I wanted to know what
weight the government attached to it:

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
speechtext:
That will appear in
season.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS

speechtext: On the orders of the day.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. W. L. MACKENZIE KING (Leader of the Opposition):
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I have in my
hand a statement not of an intended happening but of an actual happening. It refers to a policy which may be intended but which up to the present is not an actual policy. Perhaps the Prime Minister would give the house some information with respect to the facts. The Ottawa Journal of this morning prints a despatch from Washington by Ken Clark, a Canadian Press staff writer. It is as follows:
The United States government expects it will very soon receive a note from Ottawa favourably replying to the suggestion contained in Washington's note of last September that now is the time to go ahead with the St. Lawrence
Hon It. J. Manion, Canadian Minister ol Railways and Canals, told Secretary of State Henry L. Stimson, Saturday, that it is understood that while he could not speak for the Ottawa government, it was his impression that a reply might be expected in the near future. Dr Manion pointed out, it is said, that Premier Bennett had favourably mentioned the bt. Lawrence in his campaign speeches.
I need not quote the remainder of the despatch, but I would like to learn from the Prime Minister whether or not the Minister of Railways and Canals was authorized in the absence of a minister plenipotentiary at Washington to call upon the hon. the Secretary of State of the United States and to discuss with him matters pertaining to this country. I would like to know whether the Prime Minister himself will give the house any assurance as to the hope expressed in this despatch that the St. Lawrence waterway project will be proceeded with very shortly.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. R. B. BENNETT (Prime Minister) :
speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: I, too, saw the despatch to which the right hon. gentleman has referred. I was aware that my colleague the Minister of Railways and Canals had accepted an invitation of the Gridiron club to attend a dinner at Washington.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
But he never
attended it.

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
I am coming to that;
there was no dinner. The Minister of Railways and Canals travelled to Washington with the American minister to Canada. However, owing to the death of Mr. Speaker Long-worth of the House of Representatives, the dinner was postponed. My colleague assures me that he was asked as a matter of courtesy to call upon the President of the United States and several of the public officers. In accordance with that invitation he called but no matters of public business were discussed. There is no doubt that the hon. gentleman had no authority to discuss these matters or any matters of public concern on his visit to Washington. It was purely a social and personal visit to attend a dinner which did not materialize. However the minister was enabled to enjoy a very pleasant ride to Washington by air and thus to realize the advances made in scientific travel during the last few years.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
May I ask
the Prime Minister if, when the dinner is held, the Minister of Railways and Canals will be permitted to fly over again?

speakerposition: Prime Minister; Minister of Finance and Receiver General; President of the Privy Council; Secretary of State for External Affairs
maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext:
While I know my right
hon. friend does not intend me to take that question seriously, I have no doubt that if an invitation were courteously extended to him bv the American minister who accompanied him to Washington by air flight, the Minister of Railways and Canals with his usual courtesy would feel honoured to accept such an invitation.

maintopic: ST. LAWRENCE WATERWAY VISIT TO WASHINGTON OF THE MINISTER OF RAILWAYS AND CANALS
speechtext: There were contrary winds at the beginning of the flight.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext: The house resumed from Friday, March 27, consideration of the motion of Mr. Max D. Cormier for an address to His Excellency the Administrator in reply to his speech at the opening of the session, and the .proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Mackenzie King.
The Address-Mr. Dupre

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, with your
kind permission, my first words spoken within these walls, filled with memories of the deeds of our great parliamentarians, will be in the French language. My first wish is to convey, in peace and harmony, to you, Mr. Speaker, to my distinguished leader (the right hon. Mr. Bennett), to the distinguished leader of the opposition (the right hon. Mr. Mackenzie King) and to all my colleagues on both sides of the house, the cordial and fraternal greetings of the province of Quebec. However, I wished to make my bow in the house, in the language of my forebears who have been, so to speak, rooted to this soil for more than ten generations, in the language of my father and mother, in the tongue spoken from childhood by my better-half and our children, before any other language. We cherish that language because it is part of our heritage, part of ourselves, and never shall we permit it to be threatened by whomsoever it may be, whether he be a constituent, a member or even a prime minister of a province.
May I here address a few words of thanks and gratitude to my constituents of Quebec West, who, after fifty-two years of allegiance to the Liberal party, have returned to the Conservative policy.
I equally extend my congratulations to my hon. friends from Dorchester (Mr. Gagnon), Regina (Mr. Turnbull), Restigouche-Mada-waska (Mr. Cormier) and North Grey (Mr. Porteous) whose debut in the house this year and last year have been most promising.
May I at this time be permitted to continue in the other official language because the ideas I wish to express I have already dealt with in my own province. My first remarks apply to maiden speeches. Worse than the torture of the dark ages is the torture of the maiden speech. I submit such a practice should be abolished and that we should all make our debut with a second speech.
In passing may I congratulate all those who before me have gone through such a/i ordeal. Every one of them on both sides of the house has come out with flying colours; although at times some of the colours were a little too red for those sitting on your right, Mr. Speaker.
I would like to congratulate my distinguished friend the honourable ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) on his recovery. We are very happy to see him back in the house with his old fighting spirit. He likes to fight; so do we. And since my hon. friend told us in a very stem and tragical voice that he was going to continue his speech some time, some-
where, may I reply to him that we shall be very glad to answer him any time, anywhere. In his eloquent address he said:
The government is the by-product of financial depression. My hon. friends opposite are its offspring.
These are nothing but witty remarks. If I wanted to follow my hon. friend on this ground I would recall the nine years of the Liberal regime, and, imitating him, I would say: Here are the idle talkers of Canada, here are the apostles of power at any price. And if I wanted to recall the prejudices and cries of war raised against the Conservatives in the elections of 1921, 1925, 1926 and the roorback of Friday 25th of July, 1930, I would say, always imitating my hon. friend; here are the by-products of war; here are the political and electoral war babies.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Will my hon. friend tell me if he was defeated on that account in 1925?

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I am afraid so, and by the hon. gentleman himself. I could recall his story about the Germans and the Conservative party, which story was repeated in every address he delivered in the constituency of Kamouraska over a period of thirty days.
May I be permitted also, Mr. Speaker, to tell this honourable house of my first impression when I took charge of my department. I was amazed by the increasing number of prisoners in our penitentiaries and gaols This is not the proper time to decide oa whose shoulders the responsibility lies, but I submit that the practice of importing a certain class of immigrants without proper and severe selection should be corrected. The restriction on immigration imposed last August must be welcomed not only because it relieves unemployment, but also because it will tend to curtail the importation of a few undesirable elements. But in making these remarks I want it very clearly understood that I realize the important contribution made to our Canadian life and culture by the great majority of those who have come from other countries to establish their homes here.
Now, I pass to the Imperial conference. May I congratulate the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on his recent speech in this debate. I am sure the right hon. gentleman will long remain at the head of the opposition. He is not a constructive, but quite a literary critic. He is still working on lines of approach. He ought to write more books; and more books should be dedicated to him.
In his remarkable speech my right hon. friend sought at length to demonstrate that

The Address-Mr. Dupre
the attitude of the right hon. Prime Minister at the Imperial conference was not well received in Great Britain, that the relations between our country and Great Britain are not of the most harmonious character; that the policy submitted by the Prime Minister was wrong, and that his methods were wrong. May I say to the right hon. leader of the opposition that while I believe he is quite sincere'in his criticism, I am afraid that his contentions are a little at variance with reality. May I quote to the house a few expressions of opinion on the attitude of our Prime Minister at the Imperial conference.
The London Times, one of the world's great newspapers, said, and I think this will interest my right hon. friend:
The country will insist that the proposals now made by Canada shall be thoroughly examined. It is tired of empty rhetoric about mutual help and understanding and is determined to give sympathetic consideration to a concrete plan for practical cooperation now that such a plan has been definitely put before it.
The Scotsman had this to say, very likely answering, in anticipation, the remarks of the hon. the ex-Minister of Justice:
An offer was made to the mother country by representatives of the dominions, which, if accepted, would go far towards knitting the Empire together as an economic unity and so assuring its permanence and prosperity.
Xow may I draw the attention of my hon. friend the brilliant ex-Minister of National Defence (Mr. Ralston) to my next quotation; I am afraid my hon. friend was not very happy in referring us to the Manchester Guardian. This is important because I have been told that he had been designated as the probable successor to the right hon. leader of the opposition in case any political accident should happen to the latter. Of course, I hasten to add that I sincerely hope no such accident will ever occur. But my hon. friend in a moment of absent-mindedness seems to have forgotten the following statements which appeared in the Manchester Guardian. Harold Cox in the Manchester Guardian of October 10th recalled Sir Wilfrid Laurier's proposal in 1902 and commented:
This is exactly what Mr. Bennett proposes to-day. and he states his attitude with commendable frankness.
The same issue of the Manchester Guardian contains a statement by the National Council of Industry and Commerce from which I quote the following passages:
The dominions have given the mother country a great and a courageous lead by putting forth constructive proposals in clear and unmistakable terms. We are convinced that the great majority of the British people are with them.
The dominions have made a frank offer in clear and business-like terms. The policy suggested spells union and prosperity for all parts of the empire. Have we the sane business sense to accept the offer or must we permit the real wishes of our nation to be smothered with the obsolete dogmas which for successive years have proved their utter uselessness to all except the unpractical theorist and doctrinaires.
Not only the newspapers of the largest centres commented favourably, but the Bristol Evening World of October 9 in its its leading article, which might well be read by those two friends of the Liberal party, Orestes and Pylades-the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) and the hon. member for Rimouski (Sir Eugene Fiset)-says: Business men will appreciate the practicality of Mr. R. B. Bennett, Prime Minister of Canada, who, at the Imperial conference, got down to brass tacks and made a definite proposition to Britain and the dominions.
Theories that in the atmosphere of debate appear desirable may be exploded by such methods. The great value of Mr. Bennett's definiteness is that theorizing must now end, and action take its place.
Mr. Bennett's problem is not a sentimental one. He wants to sell Canadian wheat in the British and empire markets. He wants to do this not for the good of Britain or the empire but for the good of Canada. He admits he places Canada first and he expects a similar attitude tow'ard their own country on the part of other delegates.
The Bath Chronicle and Herald of October 9 states:
Mr. Bennett, the Canadian Premier, has put to the conference a proposal which does indicate a way to the solution of the big empire problem.
The Evening Sentinel of Hanley, in its leading article of October 13, says:
No truer phrase has been uttered than that of R. 15. Bennett, the Prime Minister of Canada. The time for action has come.
The Nottingham Guardian, in its comment of October 9, says:
It is to be hoped that the government will give their fullest attention to Mr. Bennett's remarkable proposal, for, in the earnest words with which he closed his speech, the time is now at hand when the doctrine of closer empire economic association must be embraced if we w'ould not have it slip forever beyond our powers of recall.
The Bristol Times and Mirror, in its issue of October 10, 1930, says:
Mr. Bennett, however, has cut into the extreme of compliments and vague aspirations with a practical proposition which he desires to be examined thoroughly by experts.
The Brixton Free Press comments in its issue of October 10, which might be interesting to my hon. friend from Temiscouata (Mr. Pouliot), as follows:
The Address-Mr. Dupre

The dominions know what the empire needs, and now they have made a definite proposal to show how an all round betterment can be secured. There is no excuse for them now. The lead has been given by the Canadian Premier.
Just to please my hon. friends opposite perhaps I might quote one of the greatest journalists of the empire, Mr. J. L. Garvin, whose comment appears in the Observer of October 12, 1930. I might direct the attention of one of the great journalists and orators of the province of Quebec, the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa), to this quotation:
On Wednesday the conference assembled at the Foreign Office to get down to business. The overseas statesmen spoke with the unprecedented frankness required at this juncture. One and all, they explained the only policy that oan be useful to them and us-extended preference for British manufactures in their markets and broad reciprocal preference for Dominion staples in ours. Other methods may be supplementary, but they must be subsidiary. Nothing but preference all round can establish a foundation for the closer economic cooperation of the empire. Mr. R. B. Bennett, for Canada, led the line. The vital thing now is acceptance or rejection of the principle. Mr. Scullin, for Australia, spoke with thoroughness and decision for the principle. Mr. Forbes, for New Zealand, Mr. Havenga, for South Africa. Mr. McGilligan, for the Irish Free State, and Sir Richard Squires, for Newfoundland, followed in the same sense. India is more reserved. But why? Because India means to be more and more protectionist. There is absolute unanimity outside the Mother Country that nothing can be done on free trade lines.
Now I should like to refer the house to a remarkable article appearing in the National Review for October, 1930, written by Right Hon. Mr. Amery, former Secretary of State for Dominion Affairs, who says:
Great, however, as was the individual and cumulative effect of the other speeches, Mr. Bennett's speech was undoubtedly the outstanding feature of the discussion in its directness and in its insistence on a decision. If he had been dealing with some new proposal his attitude might have been open to criticism as too peremptory, but on a Subject discussed at imperial conferences for over forty years, and
isille in British politics for nearly thirty, Mr. Bennett was fully justified in insisting that this country must now make up its mind one way or another without further delay.
During the last election campaign, Mr. Speaker, the hon. gentlemen opposite were saying sometimes, somewhere, "Why vote for the Conservative party on the eve of the Imperial conference? If elected to power, who would the Conservatives send to the Imperial conference?"

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I should like to ask a short question of the hon. gentleman. I should like him to be good enough to answer the article published by that good Tory paper, the

Montreal Gazette, on November 12 1930, in which it is said that the members of the Imperial conference have succeeded in doing nothing in particular and in doing it very well.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I admit, sir, that I was the weak member of the delegation, but I will say this: The Liberal party was very fortunate in having such a great statesman and high personality as Sir Wilfrid Laurier to represent Canada at several imperial conferences. However, while Canadians have every reason to be proud of all past Canadian delegations, whether Liberal or Conservative, the general opinion in London was that never did Canada send a stronger and more competent delegation than the one composed of the right hon. Prime Minister, the Minister of Justice and the Minister of Trade and Commerce. All Canadians abroad were very proud of the enthusiastic and hearty reception given our Prime Minister either at 10 Downing Street, the Foreign Office, the Guildhall or any other public meeting. This hearty and enthusiastic reception extended not only to the individual personality of our Prime Minister but also to the doctrines by him propounded. The point I wish to emphasize, however, is that public opinion in London favoured our chief doctrines, as did the industrial, financial and commercial institutions throughout the country.
Now would you like to know the explanation of the Liberal press as to this unanimity of opinion among the dominions? Here is a translation of an extract from Le Soleil, the paper of my hon. friend from Temiscouata, Mr. Pouliot) under date of Wednesday March 18: '
To these definite charges Mr. Bennett replies by two childish arguments. To begin with, he says that all the representatives of the other dominions approved of his attitude. Could they do otherwise? For the sake of solidarity, through ordinary courtesy, they could not raise any objections to the imperious, even dictatorial proposition which Mr. Bennett offered to England. T^e Prime Minister of Canada had taken the lead. He had charged bullheaded upon the English section of the conference. The others had to follow through esprit de corps.
The representatives of our sister dominions will surely be flattered at Le Soleil's conception of the motives which inspired their representations on behalf of their respective countries. The leading statesmen of the great British commonwealth of nations, or British Empire, call it whatever you like, are pictured as a bunch of cowering school boys, ready to do or say anything in order to cover a break made by the head boy.

The Address-Mr. Dupre
I wish now to refer to a very unpleasant matter. Questions of race and religion must be debated with the greatest care, and I realize that I am treading on very delicate ground. But since this is my first appearance on this great scene of our parliamentary life, I feel it is my duty to say how much I regret the attitude taken recently, and even during the last eighteen months, by a coalition government in one of the western provinces. The laws enacted against the French language- one of the two official languages-by the government of Saskatchewan are an insult to the true Canadians established here for fourteen or fifteen generations. It was in the name of God, but in the French language, that the first cross was consecrated on Canadian soil. Against these laws I must protest, and I hope they will be repealed.
May I remind public men generally that in the long run the only school which will always triumph is the school of justice, fair play, tolerance and broadmindedness.
The Canadian of French descent is the most thorough Canadian of the land; his only home is Canada. In Canada he was born, and in Canada he desires to die, faithful to his king and proud of British institutions: "Pro rege, lege, grege." But he cannot stand being molested.
Just one word now about the Russian embargo. Let us assume that thereby Canada may lose a few dollars. I submit, sir, that this question should be envisaged from the point of view of Christian morality and civilization, and may I say that I am very much surprised at the attitude taken by such important and well-written Liberal papers as the Ottawa Citizen, the Manitoba Free Press and a few others.
I see also that the Liberal party, through one of its outstanding lieutenants, my hon. friend from Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie), has taken a stand in this matter. In his most able address my hon. friend said this:
I wish to say a word or two in regard to the Russian situation which has been mentioned so frequently during the debate. Frankly I may say to the administration that possibly I appreciate very fully the motives which underlie the adoption of this policy. On the other hand, sir, in view of statements we have heard during the debate I think it is the most fatuous policy ever adopted by a supposedly sane and sensible administration.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
I notice the applause which greets this quotation from my hon. friend's speech.
But you see, on the other hand, the provincial Liberal party in Quebec declaring itself in favour of our policy. It means this: It is the old game of the Liberal party-for the embargo in Quebec, against it in Ottawa; free traders in the west, protectionists in the east; for and against conscription at the same time. On the contrary, sir, the Conservative party is unanimous in proclaiming the Russian embargo, at the present time and under the present circumstances, and on that question we are ready to stand or fall. Now we know where we are. Now you see, sitting at your left, Mr. Speaker, not the prophets, major or minor; they could not even see the unemployment crisis when it was under their very eyes. But there, at your left, sir, you see the protagonists of Russia's policy and the unconscious or conscious agents of soviet propaganda.
As already said, this is a business government for business men, for the working man and the farmer. At your right, Mr. Speaker, you see a party ready to act, to master problems, not to avoid them-a party who preaich and practise one doctrine in which they believe. On the other hand, to your left, is another party which belongs to the old school of laissez faire-avoid issues.

The Address-Mr. Dupre

that that bloc, engendered by appeals to prejudices and maintained and strengthened by detestable manoeuvres, is a thing of the past. And I say that a solid bloc, whether in Quebec or in Ontario, whether Conservative or Liberal, is a danger to unity and bonne entente in Canada. To my distinguished chief we now come, for the first time since 1917, a loyal Conservative contingent from French-speaking Quebec, and we come here to work with the great successor to Macdonald. Cartier, Thompson, Tapper, Borden and Meighen and. with him and my hon. colleagues of the cabinet, to serve the cause of prosperity.
The home has to be built. The materials are ready and the builder has been chosen by the electors. Let us work and build. If we start to discuss the rights and wrongs- and the country knows how much we, the Conservatives from Quebec, could say on the question of prejudices and cries of war raised against us-if we try to discover who have made more appeals to prejudices during the last campaign, or during the campaigns before, there will be no end to the discussion; and during such a harmful controversy the working men will be waiting for more work and the poor will be eager for additional relief.
Let us have less discussion and more action. The burden is heavy and the task formidable; but French-speaking Quebec which has known hardship and even persecutions will not shirk its duty.
Now that Their Excellencies Lord and Lady Bessborough are here, representing as they do the union of France and England, those two great nations which have played such an important part in the history of the world, let us join hands in a friendly clasp and try to solve the tremendous problems that confront us, solutions for which must be found.
Let us, the offspring of worthy sires from both sides of the channel, recall and apply to our own beloved Canada the words which Shakespeare, in Henry V, puts in the mouth of the King of France as he grants the hand of his daughter to the King of England:
Take her, fair son; and from her blood raise up
Issue to me; that the contending kingdoms Of France and England, whose very shores look pale
With envy of each other's happiness,
May cease their hatred; and this dear conjuction
Plant neighbourhood and Christian-like accord In their sweet bosoms, that never war advance
His bleeding sword 'twixt England and fair France.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, this would seem to be an opportune time to give a short resume of the general characteristics and high lights of this interesting debate. I think I am within the facts in saying that the general tenor and character of the debate have been on a par with the average of similar debates during the last ten years, and have been characterized by such moderation as is consistent with the bringing out of the facts.
Hon. members supporting the government, especially the colleagues of the right hon. the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett), have seemed to be in difficulty in defending their leader. During the first two weeks of the debate not one colleague of the Prime Minister rose in his place to defend either his leader's policies at home or his remarkable performance abroad. The hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) made a very nice speech which we all liked, but he offered no defence of his leader. The hon. Solicitor General (Mr. Dupre) made a very excellent speech, but he quoted from newspapers which were many months old. If he would peruse the press of to-day he would find that the view taken is entirely different.
Another outstanding feature of the debate is the suddenness with which the Prime Minister makes a buck dart for the curtains and lobby the moment the debate commences. In these exits he is usually accompanied by the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) and it is anything but inspiring to have to speak to these two empty seats.
Only recently the ministerial press has been complaining that the opposition has offered no alternatives to the program presented by the government.. I think that is the greatest tribute which could be made, in having the government appeal to us for an alternative policy. It is a striking admission, however, of shortcoming on the part of the government when they are forced to throw up their hands and admit a breakdown in their defences.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY

speechtext:
My hon. friends laugh, but that is as I see it. No defence has been offered by any colleague of the Prime Minister while abroad, up to this, the fifth week of this debate.
In replying to the complaint which has been made that no alternative suggestions have been offered, I would refer to the most excellent, comprehensive, telling and impelling 3peech made by the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). The right hon. gen-

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
tleman offered the suggestion that possibly the wheat exporting countries would get together to discuss the disposition of their surplus wheat, and pointed out that at such a conference we would be at a disadvantage because of the embargo which has been placed upon Russian goods; and now a conference has been called.
The hon. member for South Battleford (Mr. Vallance) made some valuable suggestions. He asked for the production of the papers in connection with the disposition of our wheat surplus during 1917 and 1918. A large surplus was disposed of at that time, and the production of the correspondence between Mr. Whiteside and the then Minister of Trade and Commerce would show that some $80,000,000 went into the treasury of the Dominion of Canada. We want to know what became of that money. We want to know also what action is being taken in connection with the representations made by hon. members from the west and by the provincial premiers with regard to the pegging of wheat for the purpose of stabilizing prices. In 1917 and 1918 the government had no hesitation in pegging wheat prices in order to prevent their going too high, but this government seems to hesitate to peg prices when they would seem to be going too low. However, they have no hesitation in pegging the prices of eastern commodities. Scarcely a week passes but the Minister of National Revenue (Mr. Ryck-man) pegs the prices of such commodities as gasoline, coal, and so on. This government has no hesitation in pegging prices for the eastern industries but will not take any action which would benefit the farmers of the west. What is sauce for the eastern goose should be sauce for the western gander, and the gander needs it pretty badly just now.
A number of other recommendations were made. The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) made a suggestion with respect to the establishment of an experimental packing plant in the west and another one in the *east. This matter has been considered on many occasions, the last being last year when a conference was held in the department over which I presided at that time. The general feeling was that before any permanent policy was laid down there should be an investigation into the whole live stock industry. In the last supplementary estimates' an item of $25,000 was included for the purpose of prosecuting such an inquiry, but the net result is that we have three different policies, a federal, a provincial and a Canadian Credit Association policy. Three different policies cannot be carried out concurrently without considerable conflict.
I would suggest that the Minister of Agriculture give more consideration to the establishment throughout Canada of additional cold storage plants. The producers of fruit and other perishable commodities, especially in British Columbia, all will testify to the value of these cold storage facilities.
In the various manifestos issued by my good friend, my successor in office, I see no reference to cooperative marketing. He should not be discouraged because there is at this time a great world wide depression adversly affecting all methods of marketing. This type of marketing will eventually offer one of the greatest hopes to the farmers of Canada. I have made a few suggestions and I hope some of them and also some of those made by other members will be found worthy of consideration. If need be, further suggestions may be made as regards desirable policies to follow.
If the Prime Minister were in his seat I should like to address some remarks to him. He has launched into the field of international affairs and diplomacy and his first experience has been quite a hectic one. Somebody has defined a diplomat to be one who could bring home the bacon without spilling the beans. If that were the correct definition I am afraid my right hon. friend would not qualify, because no other Canadian coming back from any conference has brought back less bacon and spilled more beans than my right hon. friend as he blundered abroad. I think my hon. friends opposite, by their silence, indicate their assent to that. As was pointed out by my leader in his excellent address, the mission for which they went overseas was foredoomed to failure because of the large increases in the British preferential rate. This conference, as they said, was to be a good will affair; it was to promote inter-empire trade by putting up a tariff wall. With their voice the government professed to be strongly attached to the principle of inter-empire trade, and then by their actions they banged up the tariff door against British goods as a starter. Having done that and foredoomed their case, they proceeded debonairly across the water to engage in a conference with the other members of the British commonwealth of nations.
We thought this was to be a conference, but apparently it was a speech-making proposition. One week after his arrival the leader of the government made a pronouncement, not to the conference only, but to the gallery of the entire world. I remember when this speech went over the wires and the radio to the west. We had never before heard anybody speak like this at a conference. This was, as the New York Times indicated, like an ultimatum. We wondered whether anything had gone

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
wrong with the Prime Minister, whether there was such a thing as political rabies, and whether he had contracted it while crossing the waters. We were astounded and then someone feeling a little charitable said that perhaps the newspaper was wrong and we had better wait until to-morrow. The newspapers seem to be always getting my right hon. friend wrong, and we accordingly waited until the following day When the following day arrived the confusion was still worse; nobody knew what this ten per cent was. But the clouds soon rolled away and Mr. Thomas was apparently right in describing the whole proposition as humbug. Let me quote the way in which the Prime Minister of Canada put his offer to the conference. The Solicitor General did not refer to.this; he did not defend it; he quoted merely one or two of the least objectionable paragraphs of the flamboyant statement of the Prime Minister. This is what the Prime Minister said:
First, we must approve or reject the principle.
The principle has been approved and enforced for a long time by the British government in regard to some of our products and those of other dominions. He continued:
I put the question definitely to you, and definitely it should be answered. There is here no room for compromise and there is no possibility of avoiding the issue. This is a time for plain speaking, and I speak plainly when I say that the day is now at hand when the peoples of the empire must decide, once and for all-
One would think that was the last opportunity on earth. Something terrible was going to happen unless this was immediately considered and accepted.

whether our welfare lies in closer economic union or whether it does not. Delay is hazardous, further discussion of the principle is surely unnecessary. The time for action has come.
I wonder whether this sounds the same to my right hon. friend's ears as it does to mine.
I do not hear very well, but I hear this well enough to know that it is entirely out of place in a conference among kinsmen. It is flamboyant, belligerent, bellicose and pugnacious, and in fact, worse, if I could think of anything further to add. As bad as that is, it is not as bad as the next paragraph:
Projects other than the one I propose have been placed before you. They have been carefully canvassed by our delegation, and, while we would avoid anything which might savour of premature condemnation, we are constrained to state that none of them can be accepted by Canada as alternatives at all likely to achieve the purpose we have in mind.
The proposition was off then. They might as well have quit right there. Nothing but 
tariff proposals would suit the Prime Minister and all else he dismissed with an imperious wave of his lordly hand. According to him there was nothing doing, while everybody knows that the very essence, the soul of a conference, is compromise. The moment one participant takes a mulish stand like that, the proposition is off, because of the absence of give and take.
Just a word as to what will have to be done if anything is to come out of the adjourned conference to be held in Ottawa. Of course the adjournment came in handy to save the face of the government; it enabled them to go along for a little while longer. But if the Prime Minister will take a little different attitude from that which he took at the conference last September, there is no reason why some progress cannot be made. The British government and their friends are talking about the quota that my right hon. friend arbitrarily dismissed. If anything is to be done, he must back down. I know how hard it is for a man in the Prime Minister's position, when he makes a mistake, to admit it; but if he wants to obtain results he will have to assume a different tone and also be prepared to discuss other proposals that are laid before him. A quota will be better than nothing. There is no reason why we should not have a quota with the proper proportions to the dominions. It will need to be a good quota to come up to what we are now selling to the old country. For the last five years on the average we have been selling to Great Britain 170,000,000 bushels per annum. That is as much as the rest of the world buys from us, so that any quota that is adopted will need to be at least as good as that. If it is-greater, so much the better, but there will need to be a tremendous transformation in the Prime Minister before he can get any-w'here. There is no reason in the world why we cannot through the quota system make some progress towards solving the problem which is facing the dominions in regard to their wheat. As things stand now there is a cloud on the horizon in connection with the competition of Russian wheat and our embargo against Russia. What is going to happen in the west if the Russians decide to throw more wheat into British ports next fall at the same time that ours is ready to enter also? If they choose to do that in retaliation against our embargo, the com* petition that we bad last fall will be as nothing, and it is high time that we got on to a safer road than the one on which we are travelling at the present time.
With regard to the conference, there were many interesting incidents at it and after it.

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
I recall that the first trip the Prime Minister took afterwards was to Paris. How often have we heard his voice ring in this chamber with statements as to how he was going to renounce the French treaty the first time he got his hands on it, and what an excellent salesman he was going to be! Having been chaperoned by the Solicitor General he got away from Paris without any casualties, but he did not sell as much wheat by half-9 millions to 19-to France as was sold the previous year. The Prime Minister got a promise that 9,000,000 bushels of wheat would be sold to France in the following year. The records showed however that in the previous year Canada had sold 19,000,000 bushels to France. There we have an actual sale of 19,000,000 as against a promise of 9,000,000 bushels. If the hon. gentleman continues in that way he will soon sell our wheat won't he? In the meantime Hon. Mr. Thomas had been acting up. The Labour government was under criticism by the opposition and Hon. Mr. Thomas was defending the government. An hon. member asked why he did not accept the offer of the Prime Minister of Canada and in reply he stated that such an offer was the greatest conceivable humbug. His statement set the whole newspaper world agog. My hon. friends have read many newspaper clippings but I think I will have to beg the indulgence of the house to read one or two newspaper observations. I have before me an extract from the Morning Express:
Very Simply Constituted
Mr. Bennett must be very simply constituted

I do not think it means however that the right hon. gentleman is simple minded.
Mr. Bennett must be very simply constituted (says the News-Chronicle) if he imagines that any intelligent Englishman would be deluded by the proposal that we should tax our food in return for Canada's generosity in putting another tiny brick on her tariff wall against foreign imports and keeping the wall at the same effective height against British goods.
If that proposal is not humbug what is it? The Dominion premiers like to claim the right to "speak plainly" and like to exercise it. They should be able to keep a stiff upper lip when an English statesman for once in a way speaks plainly, too.
What kind of a stiff upper lip did my right hon. friend the leader of the government keep? I understand he got in touch by phone with the acting Prime Minister; if he did not he should have done so. It was his intention to learn what was to be done about the Thomas incident. If he did not get such advice he should have got it. Instead of stiffening his upper lip and taking a mild little swat like
that, the Prime Minister squealed like a stuck porcine and was heard all over the realm. That is the kind of stiff upper lip kept by my right hon. friend when he was away from home. I will not follow this incident any further as my time is limited, but in that connection I would add that Hon. Mr. Thomas might have gone much further and been quite within the truth. This offer, so-called, was the finest exhibition of doubled dyed, twice distilled hypocrisy and humbug of which I have ever heard. No wonder they were disgusted with it overseas; no wonder the Prime Minister of Great Britain said that it could not be done. No wonder these newspapers which I might quote for an hour referred unfavourably to his proposal. In the meantime his colleagues had fled to Canada. At all events the Minister of Justice (Mr. Guthrie) and the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens) returned. In connection with the Minister of Trade and Commerce I am pleased to note that he is returning to the house. Apparently they wanted as quickly as possible to place the Atlantic ocean between themselves and their rampaging Prime Minister.
Consequently when the right hon. gentleman journeyed to Belfast he was alone, with the exception of his personal retinue. He was invited to the city of Belfast, that great city of education and industry, where he was to receive a degree. The degree was well bestowed quite properly, I think, on a very distinguished gentleman. My remarks however will be confined to statements made by my right hon. friend after he had received the degree. In this country we have made a practice of tendering banquets or luncheons and the government of Northern Ireland followed that custom by giving a luncheon. The visit of the Prime Minister of Canada seemed to well warrant such procedure on their part. In the publication which I have in my hand there is the picture of the right hon. Prime Minister wearing his university robe. This picture and several comments which I intend to read are contained in the Northern Whig and Belfast Post. There are not now many whigs in Northern Ireland nor have there been for some time past. It is a Conservative paper; certainly it is not Liberal. Apparently it hates the Labour government like poison so that it must be Conservative. Its editorials clearly indicate the political leaning of the newspaper. On the front page I find our Canadian Prime Minister's reported words "Empire ties must be economic." The next paragraph in the newspaper to which I shall refer is as follows:
"I am satisfied," he said, speaking at the luncheon, "that if we do not avail ourselves of
The Address-Mr. Motherwell

the matchless opportunity that we have by reason of our far-flung empire, our fate will be the fate of other great empires of the past."
Here the Prime Minister seems to be speaking in the role of a prophet, and a most dismal one at that. Apparently it was the opinion of the right hon. gentleman that everything would be lost unless he had his way in economic and tariff matters as they affect the other units of the British commonwealth of nations. And to rub it in good and plenty the right hon. gentleman reminded his hearers at the banquet of the ill-fated Boston tea party which every British historian knows was not brought about by the fault of the American colonies but by just such that-day Toryism as my right hon. friend still represents. What excellent taste the right hon. gentleman showed when he so spoke to the people in Northern Ireland! I quote again the following from this paper:
When you are spoken to in terms of sentiment it is always well to remember that the greatest break that ever took place in our empire commenced not over sentiment-most of you will recall the tea that found lodgment in Boston harbour. It was more than sentiment -it was economies, it was business. It was the question of the entry of products and the taxation of products that went from these islands to the land now known as the United States.
While sentiment, he asserted, must always blaze a pathway, the ties that bound peoples to one another at the present day must be ties of material strands of economic strength.
Everything in the mind of the right hon. gentleman seems to be reduced to mercenary and monetary terms; all the old ideals we were taught since childhood were discarded. Why did we send so many men to the war? Was it to sell wheat or was it because of kinship with other nations embroiled in that terrible struggle?
Probably I should not take the time of the house to read further from the paper, but for fear I might be accused of putting a wrong interpretation on the remarks of the right hon. gentleman I shall read from the editorial page. These observations appeared in the Northern Whig on the occasion of the visit to Northern Ireland by the Hon. Mr. Scallin and the Hon. Mr. Forbes, following Mr. Bennett. The remarks by my right hon. friend were delivered on November 19. It took the people in Northern Ireland apparently quite a while to recover from the shock they received following the visit of the Prime Minister of Canada. However after the visit of Mr. Scullin they became greatly heartened. I quote the following from the Northern Whig of December 3, 1930:
Mr. Bennett, who led the way, perhaps unconsciously interposed a discouraging note in

suggesting that the old bonds of blood and kindship are broken, and that unless commercial ties are substituted the empire will be in danger. In all probability, however, the Canadian premier would confess to-day that in his anxiety to impress the vital importance of closer commercial ties he rather over-stated the case.
That observation of course is quite mild. Later on the editorial is as follows:
Mr. Scullin, who followed Mr. Bennett as a visitor made it abundantly evident that Australia does not support the idea of broken or even weakened bonds of blood and kinship. He declared that these bonds are the real strength of the empire, and that without them the most powerful commercial ties might prove powerless to hold its members together. Mr. Scullin's assurances dispelled the temporary cloud which Mr. Bennett's suggestion had brought up on our horizon.
Should not the two honourable ministers who struck for Canada have remained with their honourable leader? Apparently this malady of political rabies is not quarantinable. The hon. gentlemen returned to Canada leaving their leader behind. On November 28 I find the following in an editorial of the Northern Whig.
After the cold and didactic speeches in Belfast a few days ago of Mr. Bennett, the Canadian premier, who asserted that the old ties of blood and kinship between motherland and dominiohs were broken, and that if not replaced by commercial ties "the empire would share the fate of the great empires of the past,"-
I presume, Mr. Speaker, that that means the Roman empire, the Persian empire and the other empires of the past that dwindled and decayed. The right hon. gentleman conceived the British empire as dwindling and decaying if something did not happen along the lines that he was proposing at the conference. No wonder he spoke of the sands of time running out and was terrified at the prospect of even six months delay. Then the editor goes on:
-it was heartening to hear Mr. Scullin speak of those old ties as still existent and still strong. "The unity of the commonwealth of nations," he declared, "lies in the blood ties that exist between the various parts."
Then the paper said:
We would much rather take that hopeful view than the gloomy one of Mr. Bennett.
It is not surprising that our leader was wondering who the Tories were going to send to this conference. We are still wondering why they sent the ones they did send.
Well, how is the situation to be retrieved? The trip to Paris did not help any. The Belfast experience made things even worse. Now the Prime Minister had to come home. In the meantime the great and faithful of

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
the Conservative party in Toronto and Ottawa were preparing banquets to welcome the returning hero bedecked with laurels- or at least they thought so. But evidently wiser counsel prevailed-I do not know whether from here or from Toronto-because it was realized that if they banqueted their leader he would have to make a speech. And if he made a speech what was he going to tell them? Well, a bright idea occurred to somebody. Last summer the west had been pretty well stuffed with these bedtime and fairy stories of what the government was going to do to help the farmers out there. The bright idea occurred that the Prime Minister would pour down a second dose of promises and that the west would probably gulp it as some had gulped the first dose. The Prime Minister accordingly boarded the train for the west and at every divisional point a telegram would go forward to tell them that the great emancipator was on his way to the west to bring them hope and courage to hold on. We had no snow there and cars were run all the winter. Every farmer who could scrape together a dozen of eggs-I don't think a dozen would be sufficient-or a pound of butter, and buy a gallon of gasoline, cranked up his old Lizzie and headed for Regina. All roads led to Regina because a second Abraham Lincoln, a great deliverer, had come. They had a magnificent meeting, there is no question about that, and those who could not be present heard the address over the radio. The address was so well given that you could not tell it was read. My right hon. friend claims that the reporters sometimes do not get him right, and he took the precaution on this occasion to read his address. As I say, it was well read. It differed vastly from his speech of the previous summer; I suppose that was natural. The meeting was packed to suffocation; people were sitting on their toes rather than on the chairs, with expectancy. The meeting was opened by the premier of Saskatchewan and the address of welcome was seconded by the hon. member for Regina (Mr. Turnbull)-I notice he is not listening with any great pleasure now- and everything was fine-everything but the goods; that was the trouble. Well, I will not attempt to tell you, sir, what a lot of the farmers said about the speech, but I will tell you what the farmers' union said about it. Here is the heading, "Premier Bennett Speeding West.". The train could not move fast enough to get him there. Now, for fear I might not summarize the speech correctly, I had my Ottawa Journal forwarded to me.
Here is the summary which appeared in its issue of January 1, 1931. No doubt the paper was supplied with a copy of the speech before the Prime Minister went west. The speech is divided under seven headings. The first three deal with emergency measures, one of them being to supply seed grain for needy farmers -something that has been done for the last forty years. The other four deal with Mr. Bennett's hopes for the west. Let me quote:
So far as the future is concerned, Mr. Bennett's hope for the west was summed up in the following:
These are hopes held out to the farmers of the west:
4.	He has succeeded in securing better wheat marketing arrangements with France.
I have just told the house what those arrangements developed into-assuming his hope is fulfilled the promised market there will not be half as good as it was the year before. Now the next heading:
5.	He has opened negotiations with the Chinese government for the marketing of wheat in China.
Oh, I remember that night. Right then the Prime Minister proudly said that the Hon. Herbert Marler was on his way to China to negotiate a tremendous transaction with the Chinese government for the sale of Canadian wheat. It was a wonderful story. It is not surprising that he had hope of the Hon Herbert Marler doing something when wt recall how anxious the right hon. gentleman was to have him established there in the first place. How these rafters rang when the appointment was made! His faith was well-placed, but unfortunately something went astray and we are not likely to see any immediate transaction for the exportation of Canadian wheat to China. Then the next heading is No. 6:
6.	He has several trade treaties under review with the object of securing better wheat markets with the countries concerned.
The Prime Minister did not say where these countries were, but when your back is up against the wall you will catch at anything. That was not very heartening for the farmers out west. But the best is kept for the last:
7.	He promises that when grain rates are fixed on the Hudson Bay railway they will be on the basis of the Crowsnest pass rates.
That must be balm to the soul of those waiting farmers. Why, no other rates but the Crowsnest pass rates could apply. Think of any government daring to put up any other rates on their own railway after the decision of the Hon. Mr. McKeown and the Hon.

The Address-Mr. Motherwell
Frank Oliver in the Vancouver rate case, when [DOT] they decided it would be unjust discrimination to Vancouver if the Crowsnest pass rates were not applied. And undoubtedly it would be rank discrimination against Churchill if the Crowsnest pass rates were not applied. That assurance of the Prime Minister is just so much more humbug and piffle, Mr. Speaker, take it from me. I wish parliamentary procedure would allow me to say what I feel with respect to this subject. Then think how ardently the Tory party all through the years worked for the reestablishment of Crowsnest pass rates! They the Conservatives suspended those rates in 1919, and when the King government restored them in 1922 hon. gentlemen opposite fought like wildcats against the restoration. Now they have the gall to talk about that as something they did themselves. And what of Churchill itself? The Hudson Bay Railway would terminate to-day at Nelson if hon. gentlemen opposite had had their way, and it would have been a blind alley and no good to any one. There is an untold story about that Nelson business, and I hope I shall live long enough to see it revealed. We all know that Churchill would not have been selected as the terminus for the railway if my hon. friends opposite had had their way. And yet my right hon. friend and his supporters talk about Crowsnest rates being applied on the Hudson Bay railway to Churchill and expect the farmers of the west to swallow that down without a wink!
Well, the United Farmers must have sat jp nearly all night, because the meeting did not close until about ten o'clock and after that they drafted a reply which appeared in the morning issue of the Leader, together with the report of the Prime Minister's speech. Here is what it says:
"Stunned and amazed" was the description which George H. Williams [DOT]
Who I understand was a former Conservative but then was president of the farmers' union.
-president of the United Farmers of Canada, Saskatchewan section, applied to the audience which listened to the address delivered by Premier R. B. Bennett at the armouries, Tuesday night. Mr. Williams declared that the show of enthusiasm which had marked the opening of the meeting dwindled away towards the close to perfunctory applause.
Further on in the same article I find the following:
Disappointing Pronouncement
"Mr. Bennett's address was to my mind the most disappointing pronouncement that any prime minister has ever made in a time of crisis in western Canada, and this in the face
[Mr. Motherwell.}
of press forerunners which led people to believe that Mr. Bennett would offer some solid and substantial policy," Mr. Williams declared.
This is the statement of the head of the United Farmers of Saskatchewan, who recently was in Rome, presumably helping our High Commissioner to stir things up, We hope, however, this proposed new London conference eventually will turn out all right.
That was the Regina frost. You would think there could not be anything worse, but the Prime Minister returned to Ottawa and shortly afterwards we heard of the Russian embargo. I must admit that my first reaction to the Russian situation was a shrinking away. I do not like their form of government; I do not like their attitude towards religion, or at least I do not like what that attitude is said to be. I have, however, no evidence before me upon which I can intelligently consider Russia, either as to the form of government, the attitude towards their schools or the attitude towards religion. Let me appeal to your, Mr. Speaker; you feel keenly on this matter, as I do. You cannot, however, base business transactions on prejudice, and I will admit that my first feeling was prejudice. One must let his judgment have sway, if one has any, and my judgment told me that by Canada so acting we were simply cutting off our nose to spite our face and incurring a great risk. Surely if there is any use in having a British Empire, and I claim there is much use in it, we should have consulted the other parts of the empire before taking action ourselves. Surely this is a question big enough even to go before the League of Nations; but instead of following some such course of action, we madly slap Russia in the face and put on the embargo. If he is correctly reported, the Minister of National Revenue takes the ground that Canada would not stand for that kind of government. I have the report of his remarks here, but it is not worth reading. It is an offence to a great nation with which we have to live as neighbours.
