speechtext:
Avoiding the morass of political partisan controversy, Mr. Speaker, which has already engulfed too much valuable time this session, I propose to lay before the government and the house a plain, businesslike statement, so far as I am capable, of the condition of the leading

The Address-Mr. Neill
industries in the district which I represent and throughout British Columbia generally, and if possible to suggest some constructive ideas to improve the conditions of those industries. That, I take it, is the primary purpose for which my constituents sent me here.
The major industries in my district are the basic ones of farming, fishing, lumbering, coal mining and the manufacture of pulp. If we are committed to a system of protection and higher protection, I submit that these basic industries demand that protection now, rather than that we should continue to give higher protection to the combines of wealthy manufacturers of the east, who already have more than is coming to them. As proof of this I might refer to a statement which already has been put on Hansard several times, showing that the prices of the basic products of the soil and the sea have fallen from five to eight times more than the prices of the manufactured products of the eastern factories.
Dealing first with farming, the dairy industry was materially helped when Hon. Charles Dunning cancelled the New Zealand agreement with respect to butter. The dairy industry will reap the benefit of that action more fully in the future, when the supply of butter, which was rushed into Canada before the legislation became effective is exhausted. Credit must be given also to the present government for making a temporary arrangement with Australia under which butter from that country does not come into Canada except at a price of 31 or 32 cents per pound. This arrangement is temporary, however, and the dairymen are looking anxiously for the new treaty to discover what is going to be done about imports of butter, mutton, tallow, honey and so on. Four or five months ago we heard a great deal about this Australian treaty; to read the press at that time one would think the treaty was practically negotiated. But I find nothing whatever about it in the speech from the throne. Goodness knows there is not so very much in the speech but that it would have been strengthened by a statement as to the Australian treaty. I am quite ready to remember that the Minister of Trade and Commerce (Mr. Stevens), who was negotiating the treaty, has been ill. We all hope for his speedy return to the house, but reports as to this treaty appeared in the papers long before his illness overtook him, and in any case the government goes on as a whole and it should have been possible to make mention of such an important matter in the speech from the throne. From what the leader of the government said to-day, however, it would seem that we cannot look for any action in that regard this session.
The poultry industry, which is important in British Columbia was helped also by Mr. Dunning when he raised the duty on eggs coming from the United States to 10 cents per dozen, through the countervailing duties The present government, while repealing the countervailing duties, confirmed that rate of 10 cents a dozen and made it a permanent item in the tariff. That has been a great help to the poultry industry and has practically stopped the importation of American eggs. It might be easy for me to say now that the present low price of eggs has come about because of the tariff, but that is not the fact; *it has come about in spite of the tariff. However that does show that the tariff is not a panacea for every ailment from which the *body politic can suffer, especially when we run up against high production coupled with low consumption.
What can be done to help these two major branches of agriculture? I would suggest three things, not as cure-alls, but as proposals which, in my opinion, would substantially help the situation. The first is a material advance in cooperation. The late Minister of Agriculture introduced into his department the beginning of a branch having to do with cooperation, and secured a capable man to attend to it. That should be largely developed; farmers should be encouraged, informed and trained, so to speak, to go into cooperation much more extensively than is the case at the present time. They should be educated in cooperation in the selling of their products, which is more important perhaps, than cooperation in buying. They should be trained also in cooperation in buying and in the processing of their products, in order to get them to market more cheaply. Above all, they should be educated in cooperation in the distribution of their products, because that is where a great loss occurs. As one man said, we want to cut the costs from the land to the larder. Cooperation would do away with a great deal of our present trouble.
The second grievance under which we are suffering is an old question, but it is extremely important; I refer to freight rates. We pay $4.20 per ton more for bringing wheat from the prairies for consumption in British Columbia than is paid for wheat which is to be shipped to China or Great Britain. The high rate is put upon the low grade wheat for domestic use and the low rate upon the high grade, exportable wheat, making it doubly unfair. We used to hear about the railways putting on all that the traffic would stand, but in this case they are putting on more than the traffic will stand. This ques-
The Address-Mr. Neill

tion has been before the Board of Railway Commissioners, and has been carried to the Canadian privy council, which is the government. It was taken to the privy council nearly a year ago, or perhaps more than a year ago. The last government dallied with it and did not give a decision, and the present government seem to be doing the same thing. It is time they took some action. If they do not feel called upon to deal with the matter on their own initiative by order in council, then they can bring down legislation as was done in the case of the Crowsnest rates.
It has been asserted, whenever this question has come up, that it is customary to give a preference to exportable produce of any kind. Yes, that is so in many instances; but you will find it is nearly always so when there is an alternative water route to compete, and when it is necessary to make one route compete against the other. There is no water route betwen the prairies and British Columbia, and if anything else were needed to show the injustice of the thing it is this: Since the Hon. John Oliver took up the question twelve or fifteen years ago-he fought it at every stage of the game-twice in that period there have been reductions in the export rate, but he did not succeed in getting a corresponding reduction in the domestic rate.
We will say for the sake of argument, but only for argument, because I do not admit it, that the spread fifteen years ago between the export and the domestic rates, was a proper one; but by no reasoning or logic, or lack of logic, can it be argued that the spread is right and proper now, because the export rate has been reduced twice while the domestic rate has not been reduced at alb in that period. We find nothing of this in the speech from the throne, and it is a subject of major importance and one which should find a place there. We can only suppose-I hope I am wrong-that it is not the intention of the government to deal with the matter in the immediate future.
These two things, the development of cooperation to a large extent, and the question of rates, would help the dairying and poultry industry very considerably. Ir, would enab^ them to produce cheaper and to cut the cos' in the world's market, at a time when the purchasing power of ordinary people has been much reduced.
There is another item I would suggest although it is perhaps more confined tn British Columbia. It is this. A great deal of th = coast country of British Columbia and Vancouver island, is or has been heavily timbered and before the land can be made available for agriculture it has to be cleared and

stumped; and even under present scientific methods this is very expensi\re. It costs roughly, to clear it, five times what it is worth after it is cleared, because it is not first class land, although it is good second class land Consequently it naturally holds back enormously the development of the country
I discussed the matter with the late government last year and got from them some promise that they would try to induce the National Research Council to investigate whether some method could not be devised of providing a cheap chemical which would enable these stumps to be burned out. A chemical of that kind can be obtained now, but it is too costly, and some tentative promise was made that the matter would be investigated. But little has been done. They tell me that there are other projects showing more promise of achievement which they think should be given attention first. That may be; but I would urge the government to consider the question. It would be of enormous benefit. There are a large number of soldier settlers just on the verge of insolvency, under debt to the Department of Soldiers' Civil Re-establishment, and a chemical such as I suggest would help them to get out of their financial difficulties. Furthermore, the government owns areas of these reverted lands, and there is going to be a great loss on them. It would enable the government to sell these lands at a reasonable price and, moreover, it would be a very substantial contribution to the relief of unemployment, because it would furnish a great extent of fairly cheap land. One has no idea of the large area_ which is in that condition, logged-off lands with stumps in them, which could be immediately available for people to make a living on them. At the present time it is little better than a crime to invite people to go on that land, and ask them to clear it at a cost five or six times what the land is worth after it is cleared. If this land could be cleared as I suggest, it would materially help the agricultural situation.
I come now to another industry which is absolutely unprotected, that of coal. It is suffering from competition with fuel oil. It is suggested that we should have a duty on fuel oil. At one time that would have been immediately effective, but it is somewhat doubtful whether it would work at the present time. In days gone by, all fuel oil used in British Columbia was imported, and a duty on it would have restricted its use. Now it is nearly all-and it will apparently soon be all-manufactured in British Columbia. It is manufactured through the production c"

The Address-Mr. Neill
gasoline out of crude oil. It is a by-product, and it is doubtful whether a duty would have the desired effect, because the manufacturers treat this oil as a by-product. They make their money on gasoline, and it might be that if a duty were placed on fuel oil they would sell it for whatever they could get for it and they would cut the price to the extent of the duty. That would mean that the government would get an income, but it would be of no benefit to the coal industry, which is what we want to help. That is a matter which the government experts might inquire into.
Now there is an immediate and certain remedy. I emphasize those words because it cannot be denied that it would have an effect the moment it was put into force, and I urge the necessitiy for immediate action inasmuch as the industry is in a desperate condition. What I suggest is this: that the government grant a bonus of $1.50 a ton on all coal mined in Vancouver island for export purposes other than to the United States. I leave out the east of British Columbia because they share in certain favourable rates granted Alberta. I leave out coal for domestic purposes in British Columbia and also coal for export to the United States, as there is a reciprocal condition there which would not benefit us. I am speaking merely of coal for other export. There is a precedent for it. Nova Scotia gets a railway rate to allow it to get into the markets of Ontario, and Alberta gets a rate which is sometimes quoted as $1.25, although it is $1.48, and it is apt to be more than that because it is on a sliding scale. That is what the country at large pays to make up the difference between the rate granted Alberta and eastern British Columbia coal and what it costs the railway company. The first period calculated, as I say, came to $1.48 a ton. And what is it for? To enable coal to be moved to the desired market in Ontario. Now, we suggest that a bonus of this description would enable us to export coal to the markets of South America-Peru, Chile, Valparaiso. It would not be a great drain on the treasury to begin with, and we believe it would develop more trade.
In this connection we also ask for some cooperation from the government, more particularly from the Department of Marine. I am sorry the minister is not present. A father can flog his child for lying to him, but unless he sets an example of personal rectitude he will not do much more than make the boy a hypocrite. And this is the situation here. There is a boat called The
Lillooet, under the control of the Marine department. It has been operating on the Pacific ocean on a hydrographic survey. Some years ago the department proposed to turn it into a oil burner and I opposed this. With the help of the late Hon. Mr. Sloan, a member of the provincial government and a representative of a coal-mining district, we ' got the government to abandon the idea. Now this last fall the Department of Marine decided to build another hydrographic survey ship, and the moment I heard that tenders had been called for I wrote to the minister. I wrote at once, not after it was too late, and urged him to see that the boat should be a coal burner. I am sorry to say that I have not received a reply to my letter-of such are the children of Ammon! My appeal certainly fell on stony ground, because a notice appeared in the papers a few weeks ago to the effect that the ship would be an oil burner. Then Sir Henry Thornton, the president of the Canadian National Railways, informs us that he will not allow the hotel which is being built in Vancouver to use anything but oil. And worse than that, we find them building a great tank of a million gallons capacity at Port Mann, with a view to changing a good many of theiir engines on the Canadian National Railways from coal to oil, in startling contrast with the action of the Canadian Pacific Railway, which is not under government control. A meeting of the coal operators was held last fall, at which I was present, and the agent of the Canadian Pacific promised that their switching engines in Vancouver would be changed back from oil-burning to coal-burning. This means a coal consumption of something like 20,000 tons per year. The government should continue the experiments made by the late government in the use of pulverized coal. At a recent sitting of the provincial legislature, a member moved a resolution along these lines, but the government moved an amendment suggesting a survey.
If there is one thing we do not want in this connection, it is a survey. The Government in British Columbia have gone crazy over surveys. It does not matter what the trouble is, whether it is cut worms or currency, whether it is railway rates or rabbits, if you complain the government finally says: "We will, give you a survey." The hon. members from British Columbia know what that means; it means a lot of fat jobs for political heelers and it means the postponement of action dearly beloved by the provincial government When we ask for anything during the sittin
The Address-Mr. Neill

of the legislature we are promised a survey to be made during the recess. Upon one occasion we endured such a survey and we came back at the next session and said: You have had your survey, give us action. What did they do? They ordered another, a second survey. We do not want stone, we want bread. I have argued this matter for ten years both in and out of this house, and now with desperate earnestness I say to the government: It is now or never for this industry. I have a local paper which announces that two large mines have been closed and other mines are operating on a part time basis of two and three days per week. That practice has been carried on all winter, which season is the harvest time for the coal miner. If they can only get two days work a week in winter what will be their condition in the summer? I tell the government that if no action is taken in this matter, 5,000 miners counting those dependent directly and indirectly upon them will have to be supported by relief measures. I hope the Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) will give us some action. He has never been accused, even by his worst enemies, of not being a man of action, and surely he will do something to relieve this desperate condition.
The next matter I would draw to the attention of the government is the lumber and pulp industry. This industry has reached a state where many operators are indifferent whether or not they run their camps. When the camps are run, the work is speeded up, sometimes through the efforts of the men themselves in an attempt to keep the camp going, and such overspeed means danger. The equipment is not being kept up and in many cases has reached a state where it might be called haywire. That class of equipment and speeded operations mean but one thing-increased danger, more accidents and, alas, more deaths, because in many instances the accidents prove to be fatal.
This industry sent a delegation to Australia some years ago and they received a promise of preference in the treaty soon to be negotiated. An Australian paper says that a preference on lumber as well as on fish has been given to us, and we are very anxious to see what is to become of that treaty. Up to the present, all that we can find is that nothing is to become of it. A very substantial preference was granted, something like $5 per thousand on lumber. Unfortunately, their currency has depreciated and this preference does not mean nearly as much as it would seem to. A mistake has been made in Australia, apparently through lack of information, in that while a preference has been given on Douglas fir, none has been given

on hemlock and spruce, both equally important to the industry. I hope the government will keep this fact in mind in negotiating any treaty.
The government should continue the payment of a bonus to ships on the Australian route. Because of conditions in Australia, this trade has dropped considerably and the government should do everything to encourage it.
The Commercial Intelligence Journal contains a statement that the sale of Canadian lumber in Great Britain is being handicapped because other nations are selling their lumber as Canadian. The suggestion is made that it soon may be too late to make an effort to have Canadian lumber marked as such. One of the lumber associations in British Columbia has arranged to mark their product with a trade mark, but that is not what is wanted. We want government action which will guarantee that all lumber from Canada will be marked under government control with the word "Canada" or some similar word. An attempt should be made to get the British government to make it compulsory that other lumber be marked with its country of origin. Some publicity should be given to the superiority of our Douglas fir over other competing woods, which superiority is not generally understood. Perhaps the High Commissioner, after he has completed his self-imposed task of reforming the sentiments, morals and economics of the British people, will find time to advertise Canadian lumber.
Fisheries are very important to British Columbia. The market and prices have both almost disappeared, but we are living in the hope that world industrial conditions will improve and that we shall be able again to find a reasonably profitable market for our fish. Australia has recently given us a preference on salmon amounting to something like $2.50 per case. The government should take steps to implement this preference and see that it is included in the next trade treaty.
When assistance for the fishing industry in British Columbia is mentioned, one's thoughts naturally turn to the regulations, which are changed once or twice each year. If I may suggest to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Rhodes), we would like a holiday on regulations-leave us alone for a time. We are like the soldier who lay wounded in hospital. He was being fussed over by well-meaning society ladies until finally he put up this notice: " I am too sick to be nursed to-day." I think I speak for the great majority of the working fishermen when I say that there is

The Address-Mr. Neill
one exception to this rule; we do not want the minister to abandon the system which hs inaugurated of either he or his deputy or both visiting British Columbia every fall. That is one of the finest things ever started by the department. In the old days the fishermen had no voice; the big interests formulated the policies in the minister's office. They could come to Ottawa, but the fisherman was never heard of. Some hon. member might make a protest from the floor of the house, but it was then too late. This holding of meetings of fishermen in Vancouver, Nanaimo and Prince Rupert has been of great benefit to both the industry and the department. The fishermen feel that their complaints are being listened to and that if they are reasonable, some relief will be given. I strongly recommend that these meetings be continued.
I wish to thank the minister on behalf of the industry for coming out last fall, and I desire to thank him for what he did not do on that occasion. In making this statement, I do not want it to be taken as cheap sar= casm. A small section of the industry made up their minds as to what he was going to do; every political, financial, economic and social influence was brought to bear. He was not to be allowed to take a bath without being accompanied by some of the elect. Banquets were held which only the elite were permitted to attend; he was to be supplied wiui food, flattery and fiction, and it was determined that he was to see only through their eyes. But what did they get? The minister turned out to be, in the vermicular of British Columbia, a wise guy, almost as wise as he looks. He sat and listened and drank it all in, and looked wise and the more he listened and the more he drank, the wiser he looked. That is about all they got out of him. A few days later he insisted on attending an open meeting of fishermen held in the same town, where there were no flourishes, no sycophancies, no banquets, no flowers, but he listened to the orderly presentation of the views of twenty thousand working fishermen. He listened attentively and courteously. He did not promise anything, we did not expect that; we wanted only a hearing. He went away. When the regulations came out, he had not given us much we asked for, but he had rejected the views put forward by the vested interests. There were three major proposals presented to him by them, and he was to be compelled to adopt them. He turned them down. I am prepared to say, without fear of contradiction, that if he had granted any one or all three of those things 22110-35
it would have spelled disaster and ruin to thousands of working fishermen. I must admit that the minister did fall from grace in one respect, or rather I will not say "fall", I will just say, "slipped". It was just a cog. He gave way in his regulations on two small points, unfortunately in the district which I represent. This will inure to the benefit of a gentleman who was the campaign manager of my opponent. While I chronicle that side slip, so to speak, I must admit that as regards the general industry as a whole, it was in two entirely minor matters.
If I have time there are two or three suggestions I should like to make. I have the backing of meetings of fishermen and boards of trade in asking that the minister should not give more power to the chief supervisor of fisheries in British Columbia. He has too much power already. We do not want any Mussolinis in British Columbia. Give power and authority to some officials and they rise to the occasion and become bigger and better men. Others merely-swell. Again I would say, as the minister values his reputation, let him refrain from having any part or lot with the Hon. Mr. Howe, Commissioner of Fisheries of British Columbia.

I see these words awake an echo amongst British Columbia members. He is a very nice gentleman, but his ignorance of fishery matters is appalling and his credulity is colossal. About a year ago the privy council in London gave the provincial government power to regulate the manufacture of fish after they were caught, not before. This gentleman was induced in his innocence to formulate a series of quibbling regulations by means of which he was going to wrest the power from the minister who sits opposite; he was going to take away our jurisdiction over the catching of fish. The result as regards the condition of the common fisherman would have very much resembled that in Russia. It certainly would have been economic slavery. The members of the local house, Liberals and Conservatives alike, united to fight the proposition in a committee of the local house. At last the Commissioner threw up his hands and admitted that the whole thing had been conceived by arrangement and born in ignorance. That was the end of that. A few weeks afterwards I read in one of his party papers-and I suppose it was correct-that he said his scheme was getting along nicely, but the member for Comox-Alberni had gone up and down the coast "sowing his poison" and he himself had

The Address-Mr. Neill

"reaped the whirlwind." I did not know that reaping the whirlwind was the repercussion of poison; I thought that the first reaction would be a tummy-ache. The gentleman's metaphor was very much mixed. It suggests that he has little knowledge of medicine, but I assure you, Mr. Speaker, that his knowledge of medicine is profound as compared with his knowledge, or lack of knowledge, of fishery matters. Defeated in that attempt, he has adopted another line of procedure, and is now trying to work up propaganda to get this government and parliament to hand over to him the whole of the rights o.ver the fishing industry. All I say to that is: God forbid. We do not know very much about the minister at Ottawa, but what little we do know is rather to his credit, and I think we will take this position, that we would rather have the devil at Ottawa-he will excuse the term; it is used as one of endearment-of whom we know little, than the devil at Victoria of whom we know all too much.
I do not know whether I have time to say a word on the question of fishery guardians. They are temporary men appointed for from two to five months every year. They are not *Civil Service Commission appointees, and therefore they are not entitled to the soldiers' preference by law, but surely the government will admit that they are entitled to the preference in so far as it comes under political patronage. That is to say, these men will be appointed by patronage in accordance with the custom "but I hope they will give a preference to present employees and to the returned men. .The system I followed in days gone by was that if a man had been employed for two years and there was no kick from the department as to his work he should be left on, no matter what his politics were. This gave the department good servants, efficient men, because they knew that it was not politics but attention to their duties that kept them in their positions. What is to be done to-day? I very much fear they are going to revert to a system of political appointment only. I know a man who has given six years' good service and who has been told that he will have to apply for the endorsation of the local Conservative Association. That means that some political appointee, and not even a returned man, will get the job. That is not going to make for good service. I should like to read part of a resolution passed by a soldiers' body, which, after reciting the facts outlined above, says:
Therefore the Courtenay branch of the Canadian Legion beg to recommend,-

First, that where men have held such positions for two or more years without complaint from their superior officers, they should be reappointed.
Second, that when there are vacancies, the branches of the legion in the districts where the vacancies occur (or the nearest thereto) be asked to nominate returned men suitable for the position.
I think two or three of these resolutions have been sent to the minister and I would suggest that he take the stand that those who have done good service, who' have not taken any part in politics, and especially those who are returned men, should be left alone.
I have just time for a word more regarding the Imperial conference. I regret the failure of that conference. Criticism has been made of the methods of approach and also of the result. A great deal of it I fear was true. I fear that the wisest methods were not adopted, but behind and beyond those methods is there not this fundamental cause, so to speak, namely that Canada rejected the British preference? If she had not done that the result might have been different. At least it appeared to Great Britain that- we rejected the British preference, although I do not think we did. The issue was so involved with other things that it was not possible to state the situation clearly. But Great Britain saw it in that light, and that was primarily the cause of the non-success of the conference. More diplomatic methods might have been applied. I believe in "vox populi, vox dei," in accepting the decision of the people. Nevertheless it is possible to say that I regret the decision if it was clearly against the British preference, because I think that was a mistake. Speaking from an entirely selfish, mercenary point of view_ and __for the moment as one whose horizon is bounded by a Canadian " sspectr I think it would have been better for us, better for Canada, if we had united ourselves along those close and intimate lines that trade produces, with our own kith and kin across the water rather than with the country to the south of us, who, however friendly for the moment, may at any time- and this has happened-cut all those bonds of trade and turn us loose with a disorganized trade condition on our bands from which we cannot recover for many years. Apart from any sentimental regard whatever, I think it would be better if we dealt with our own breed. I hope the day will come soon when we may secure a greater measure of British preference, which cannot but be to the mutual benefit of Canada, Great Britain and the British Empire itself.

The Address-Mr. Duguay
myself with previous speakers in congratulating the mover1 and seconder of the address in reply to the speech from the throne. I especially want to congratulate the hon. member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Cormier) for having stood up as the representative of the Acadian minority. I answer that the fault rests not only on Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but also on the Liberal party as a whole. Last year, that party had the opportunity of proving its sincerity in connection with the rights of the minority, but instead of vindicating here in this House of Commons, the rights which it haughtily proclaims in the province of Quebec, it is content to take a different attitude as I shall show by referring to last year's Hansard, at page 1699:
I think the hon. member for Labelle and the house as a whole can trust the sense of justice and fairness of the people of Alberta and Saskatchewan and their respective governments to deal generously and fairly with every class of the community.
Mr. Lapointe:	That is really what is being
done.
Mr. Speakman:	I quite appreciate that in
the terms of the argument. I am applying my remarks rather to the argument of the member for Labelle.
Mr. Lapointe:	That is really what is being
done. It_ is a, mark of our confidence in the two provinces instead of keeping this endowment fund here w'e are transferring it to them.
They then expressed their confidence in the Saskatchewan government which is the same one in power to-day. For instance, in the last general election, the Prime Minister of Quebec himself, according to the hon. member for Quebec-Montmorency (Mr. Dorion), took advantage of these prejudices against the Conservative party in Quebec. Fortunately, many Quebec ridings gave little credence to them, and, to-day, more than twenty members from that province are here to straighten things out and tell the house that Conservatives deal with the French language with equity and are happy to proclaim that, under the present government the rights of minorities are as well safeguarded as they were under the previous administration. Moreover, sir, I may state that personally I am entirely opposed to Mr. Anderson's policy and that I would never sacrifice the rights of minorities for political gain, because to me principles are above party interests.
Some hon. members opposite shouted: "Shame, shame," when they were unmasked

by the hon. member for Montmagny (Mr. LaVergne). But what do they think, for instance, of Mr. Olivar Asselin, chief editor of the Canada, a Liberal newspaper of Montreal, who wrote in his pamphlet entitled: "Sir Wilfrid Laurier", at page 8:
The Dominion cabinet, in which were still to be found a few of the fathers of confederation, for decency's sake, hesitated to definitely break off with the traditions of Macdonald and Cartier, and became alarmed. They wished to gain time, consult the courts with reference to some terms which to all men of good will-seemed quite clear. The courts having acknowledged the rights of Catholics, after years of delay, the government decided to act. The* cabinet divided. Mr. Laurier might, by adhering to the right cause have assured its triumph, and thereby might have helped in guiding the federal authorities in the right path whence they had been drifting away for ever so long. However, the opportunity of being raised to power was too alluring, it was he on the contrary who, the first, declared war, siding with the government despoiler, shouting: "Hands off Manitoba!" He was the first in this crisis, and the first since 1867, with the exception of a few fanatics whom all parties had always kept at a distance, he laid down as a principle the absolute sovereignty of provinces in matters of education. All whose sentiments were anti-Catholic and anti-French, in Canada, grouped around him.
That is what the chief editor, himself, of this Liberal newspaper of Montreal wrote at the time. When a Conservative, not long ago, stated very similar views, they shouted: "shame", yet, the author of this article, is given high praise for his editorials in the Canada and they feel proud in handing over to him the management of -this partisan newspaper.
If this is the way, sir, that the Liberals protect the rights of minorities, I am glad to see the Conservative party in power, because I am convinced that these rights are better safeguarded under Conservative than under Liberal rule.
Let us, sir, broach another subject. May I ask what in substance has been advised by our opponents since the outset of this session? They delivered many speeches. They especially proclaimed that the Conservatives had not fulfilled their pledges. May I, previous to indicating how the present government fulfilled their pledges, state what the Liberals did with theirs? At the opening of the first session of the Liberal government on March 9, 1922, the following words are put in the speech from the throne:
Whilst of the opinion that unemployment relief is fundamentally a municipal and provincial responsibility, my government has felt that as conditions have arisen in a measure out of the late w'ar, they would be justified in continuing for the period of the winter months the expedient of supplementing by grants from

The Address-Mr. Hurtubise
the federal treasury the relief or contributions of provinces and municipalities for the purpose of alleviating actual distress.
A little further in the same speech from the throne, we find:
The stream of immigration to the Dominion was much interrupted and restricted during the war. Now that the blessing of peace is with us, a renewal of efforts to bring in new settlers must be made. My government are fully alive to the importance of this question and will use every reasonable endeavour to attract to our country people of the most desirable class with particular regard to settlement on our undeveloped lands.
The Liberal government alleviated unemployment which existed in 1922 by bringing to our shores, in the space of 9 years, from 1921 to 1930, more than 1,150,000 immigrants who cost the country 820,000,000. Under the Liberal regime, the right hon. Mr. King absolutely stated that he had wiped out unemployment. Yet, a year ago, the hon. member for North Winnipeg (Mr. Heaps) requested the government to take immediate steps to relieve unemployment. What was the government's answer? I shall quote, for the benefit of members on the left who shouted: "No, no", when the hon. Postmaster General (Mr. Sauve) told them that they had denied there was any unemployment, the baffling statements of their leader, on April 3, 1930, at page 1226 of Hansard:
.... we have no right to say that there is any national unemployment problem in this country.
He went further and stated:
.... that there is no way in which you can more effectively defeat the possibility of investment of capital in your country than to seek to create the impression in other lands, and throughout your own,- that conditions are _ not prosperous, that they are bad and that there are within this country large numbers of unemployed.
Last year, mention of unemployment was not permitted, however, this year they are in the opposition and last year's scruples are set aside.
In 1922, the government wished to relieve unemployment by bringing immigrants to this country. What was the policy of the Conservative government in 1930? They admitted that unemployment existed and their first step was to stop immigration; secondly they called a conference of delegates from all the provinces; thirdly they convoked an emergency session-which was never to take place according to our opponents-and lastly they appropriated an amount of $20,000,000, thereby giving work to thousands of unemployed. Yet notwithstanding all this, we have done nothing according to our hon. friends, to alleviate the

present crisis! Hon. members in the opposition, sir, in order to belittle the acts of the present administration, unceasingly lay stress on the pledges which we made. These pledges, neither the government nor the people will forget and they will be carried out for the greatest welfare of the country.
What is very interesting also is to remind the opposition of their 1921 pledges and find out what became of them. They were, first, to force people of means to pay the war expenditure in the shape of an income tax. This tax, in 1922, brought in a revenue of $78,000,000; in 1929 under the Liberal regime, it had already decreased to $69,000,000. Instead of increasing this tax they decreased it. This was in violation of their first pledge. Then, the war expenditure was to be paid by business profit taxes. In 1922, this brought in $23,000,000; in 1929, it gave but $450,000.
The sales tax was to be abolished to help the poor ratepayers. The tax amounted to 5 per cent in 1922. TJie Liberals increased it to 6 per cent, to reduce it later to 4, 3 and 2 per cent. But thanks to these increases, the Liberals drew from the people $180,000,000 more than the Conservative administrations.
The cost of living was also to be reduced. In 1922, the weekly family budget for five people was $21.52. After nine years of Liberal administration it fell to $20.21, that is a decrease of $1.21. Labour wages are considerably lower so that living conditions are harder to-day than they were at that time. One wonders what would have happened in Canada had the Liberals remained in power.
We have been listening to their complaints, since the opening of the session, that we are doing nothing to alleviate unemployment. But what suggestion to alleviate unemployment have they made to the government? Very seldom since confederation has a government, presenting its first speech from the throne been subjected to such an avalanche of criticisms. If they are truly desirous as they proclaimed during the elections, to promote the welfare of the people and remedy unemployment, why do they, to-day, oblige the government to listen to these lengthy speeches which are devoid of all suggestion tending to alleviate unemployment? It seems to me that the best way to prove their sincerity would be to curtail the number of their speeches and ask the government to act immediately.
I should like to make suggestions, but under the present circumstances, I shall desist seeing that I expect the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) to enact measures which will be very helpful to farmers.

The Address-Mr. Hurtubise
The Quebec farmers especially are suffering from the unemployment crisis. The majority of them had no crops last year, the consequence is they feel very depressed. I hope that the measures brought down by the hon. Minister of Agriculture will be a boon to all farmers. The Lake St. John county which I am privileged to represent is anxiously awaiting these measures.
In closing my remarks, sir, I wish to state that the government may depend on my entire support and that it rejoices me to think that some day prosperity will return again to this country under the standard of the Conservative party.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, my first thought is to express a feeling of diffidence in the presence of hon. ministers of the crown and members of this house, who for the most part are my seniors in parliamentary experience. 1 .therefore, sir, beg your indulgence. At the outset, allow me to make use of the French language, it being a privilege for which I am indebted to a large number of my constituents who were the pioneers of New Ontario; settlers, artisans, manufacturers and professional men. In spite of many adversities they succeeded in having their language, usages and customs respected, and in reaching an enviable place in the community. I shall thereafter speak in English; I owe it to my English-speaking friends who have been kindness itself towards my compatriots and with whom also we form a large family, working harmoniously together for the common weal. Ho! there are among us, like in Saskatchewan, extremists who preach hatred and discord, but their number is limited and sensible people pay no attention to them. It would have given me much pleasure to be one of those who congratulated you, . Mr. Speaker, on the occasion of your election to the speakership of this house. I have full confidence that you will, sir, continue with all fairness, dignity and ability to direct the deliberations of the house. My congratulations extend also to the hon. members who moved and seconded the address in reply to the speech from the throne. It was a credit to them and I wish them success in their future career. I also want to extend my congratulations to the leader of the opposition for his splendid speech which will be handed down to posterity as the most complete, up-to-date and to the point speech in the present crisis. It will be looked upon as a "vademecum" by the Liberal members and perhaps also by the members on the opposite side. Speeches both well thought out and instructive have been delivered since the opening of the session, however, I wish to mention particularly that of the hon. member
for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand)-the riding in which I had the pleasure of polling my first Liberal vote. He vividly pictured the decline of agriculture, made worse by these few months of protection under the present administration, and he suggested the remedy for these ills. Then I would like to congratulate the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beaubien), who gave us an outline of the situation on the western farms. I entirely agree with these hon. gentlemen and I trust the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Weir) will not turn a deaf ear to those appeals and that he will soon acquaint us with the measures which, in his opinion, will remedy these conditions. We have already been waiting a few months. After all the pledges made during the last election, and especially the one with reference to the immediate relief of unemployment, what do we see? The $20,000,000 are spent; unemployment is very much in evidence everywhere the price of farm products is ever on the decrease; the elevators are still overflowing with grain, the granting of old age pensions is made conditional on the state of our finances; the highway from coast to coast which was to give work to hundreds of thousands of men has not been decided upon. To shelter themselves the Dominion government blame our provincial governments and vice versa; the deepening of the St. Lawrence channel is still under consideration and as things stand it will yet be for some years to come. The partial tariff revision enacted last, session has been so unpopular that the government has been obliged to amend or cancel almost all their decisions. Every day, through correspondence, conversation and the press protests are lodged against the raising of the tariff and we are earnestly entreated not to allow the government to have their own way during the present session. Since July, 1930, sir, the Canadian people have been expecting a well-defined policy in all the various departments, yet the ministers of the crown travel about, deliver speeches and lectures, sometimes are even present to listen to the debates in the house, but remain dumb. When shall we expect the next sequence of pledges? The hon. ministers of the crown have the floor.
I should like, Mr. Speaker, to make a few remarks in English as I feel it is my duty to present the views of my constituency, which is composed of a considerable number of farmers and also a large number of labourers employed in the mining, lumber and railway industries.
I have listened with great interest to the speech of the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King), which I believe-although its length and content and

The Address-Mr. Hurtubise
preparation did not suit the government-was the most comprehensive, detailed and elaborate that I have heard. I have also listened to the answer of the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) who spoke more laboriously than during the last electoral campaign. Many other well-prepared and interesting speeches were made by hon. members on both sides of the house. The trend of those speeches has been along the line of the promises made by the government last summer, its legislation passed thereafter, and the benefits derived therefrom.
In my part of the country the people-although the majority had great confidence in the late government's policy, and did not let themselves be humbugged by the alluring promises made my opponents-have yet to see the fulfilment of most of the promises and to experience the benefits to be derived from the legislation passed by the government since its advent to power. The farmers, who have been toiling under great difficulties for several years on account of the lack of encouragement from the provincial government, had hoped to have some temporary assistance from the 820,000,000 voted last session; but the benefits received have been far from what was expected.
I congratulate the hon. member for Prescott (Mr. Bertrand) upon the very valuable information contained in his speech. He dealt with the question of farming as a man who knows something about the cost of farm production and farm revenues. I congratulate the hon. member for Provencher (Mr. Beau-bien) on his splendid speech. I happen to know a little about the difficulties encountered by the-western farmer, as I_ have a brother in Alberta whom I visit regularly. I fully concur with the hon. member because I too believe that agriculture is the basic industry of the country, and unless something is done to check this state of marasmus-and it is not exaggerated as we were led to believe by the right hon. Prime Minister-general conditions, I submit, will continue to be more and more embarrassing for those that have the duty and the responsibility to guide the destinies of this country.
I cannot see how our farming industry can be helped otherwise than, first, by lowering the tariff and increasing the British preference, for the British market at present is the best outlet for Canadian trade since the United States and other countries have closed their doors by high tariffs; secondly, by lowering the freight rates which are such an item of cost in some parts of the country; third, by giving the farmers a low rate of interest on loans, not only to oarry them over the crisis,

but for an indefinite time until a change in rate is judged necessary; and, fourthly, by representation of agriculture on the Canadian National Railway board on account of the farmers being particularly concerned in transportation.
In northern Ontario the farmers are leaving their farms every year, not on account of extravagance in living, but on account of the high co6t of production and of the high cost of living. They have to pay more and more every year for their farm implements, automobiles, trucks, household equipment, groceries and clothing. At the last election they were led to believe that good times were around the comer and that the only way not to miss the opportunity was to vote Conservative. Then they would be able to sell their farm products at almost any price that they might ask, and in their spare time they could work on that famous trans-Canada highway and participate in the large sums of money to be voted for that purpose. Some believed it, but the majority in my county did not. To-day the farmer can get hardly anything for his butter and eggs, and the trans-Canada highway has been undertaken only at points where a few men can get a few days work at a wage that is next to slavery, as was said by my hon. friend from Kenora (Mr. Heenan) Yes, since last fall I have received letters from some describing the conditions under which they were working, and from others asking me if it was reasonable to work at wages so low as 30 cents an hour-eight hours a day, $2.40, $14.40 a week. In other places the men were employed only three days a week, thus earning only $720. I know a man who is taking legal proceedings against the northern development branch for money earned and refused to him, I have proof of this under my hand.
Labour conditions in northern Ontario have been going from bad to worse. To-day I have received my home paper, the Sudbury Star, of April 8, which contains a long statement by the chairman of the local relief committee. Let me quote the following extract:
An idea of the situation this winter may be had from the records of the relief committee. On the first of November there were 415 married men registered out of work. By December 31, this number had increased to 1,226 and on April 3 it was 1,693. On the first of November there were 498 single men registered, on December 31 there were 3,052 and on April 3, 3,438. Of this total registration there were, of course, a large number of men given part time work throughout the season.
Since the soup kitchen opened in November there have been 90,329 meals given out at an approximate cost to the city of $5,419. The

The Address-Mr. Hurtubise
kitchen is still in operation, serving an average of 425 meals a day. and the city is at present caring for 170 families.
This expense is not borne by the government, but by the local authorities. I submit this confirms my statement that labour conditions in northern Ontario have been going from bad to worse.
In 1919 there was an understanding between the Minister of Lands and Forests of Ontario and the hon. member for Kenora-Rainy River, who was then member of the provincial legislature representing the Constituency of Kenora, that in northern Ontario the wages whould be 35 cents an hour, that is, $3.50 a day, or $21 a week for all government work. At the last session, there was a promise by the government, in answer to a question by the hon. member for Kenora, that the prevailing rate of wages would be adhered to. Although this was provided for in the Unemployment Relief Act, we find that those rates have been cut down. I say that the government is in duty bound to refund the difference to the employees. We have reports from papers of March 6, 1931, that labour conditions in northern Ontario are good. Those reports are not correct. Every day I receive letters, some are anonymous, because the writers do not dare sign their names for fear of losing their pitiful jobs-describing the favoritism practiced by the friends of the government and the hardship the writers have to endure. When the Minister of Labour reports that conditions in northern Ontario are good, either he is misrepresenting the facts personally or he is being misled by his friends. The Prime Minister says conditions are improving all over the country. While this may be so in a few isolated places, in the majority of cases they are going from bad to worse. During the last campaign the Conservatives said that the federal government, which then was Liberal, would not cooperate on a fifty per cent basis, but there is nothing in the sessional papers to show that a province ever asked for help.
When I consider the psychological effect created by the propaganda of our Conservative friends during the last campaign; the unrealizable promises which were made; the policies advocated which thereafter proved impracticable and even noxious to the consumer while beneficial only to the few, it is not surprising to see so much unrest in this country and to hear so much talk about communism. I do not want to refer to the matter of trade between this country and Russia, where at present communism is being tried out, because this trade proposition seems
to be a debatable question. This is proved by the diverse expressions of opinion by financiers and leading men of Canada, and even by some hon. members of this house. Sudbury, through publicity, has the name of being a centre of communism. Probably that is so, but let me say that of the large number . of immigrants who have come to our city representing many nations, a great many have been naturalized, have adopted the laws and the ways of living of the Canadian people and to-day rank among our best citizens. They are industrious and law-abiding citizens, to whom I owe this tribute of consideration.
If there is such a state of unrest and such an attraction to communistic ideas, it is due in great part to the lack of foresight in the province in not preventing part time work in many of our industries, such as the pulp industry. It is also due to the fact that, particularly in this present crisis, the people of Canada have been living on promises. When these promises have not been fulfilled or, having been fulfilled, have proved worthless and even injurious to the mass of the people and had to be changed or cancelled, we have been told to be patient. We have been waiting, waiting and waiting, but hope deferred maketh the heart sick.
Since the opening of the session some hon. members have referred to Canada, in the present crisis, as a very sick patient. As a doctor myself, I believe the patient is very sick. In this world-wide epidemic of markets crumbling, industries closing and people walking the streets waiting anxiously for the proper advice and treatment to save them from disaster, Doctor King said, " This is going to be a serious epidemic. Let us confer so as to not make a blunder. We shall see what germs are the cause of thi3 disease, what are the reasons for these clinical symptoms and what treatment we will then apply." But Doctor Bennett came rushing in, saying, "This is no time to confer; this is a time to act. We shall use an empirical treatment. We shall first give the patient a good dose of some preparation of opium, such as 'a special session', immediate disappearance of unemployment', 'good markets for the western wheat', 'good markets for the farmers' eggs and butter', 'pensions for old age', 'the immediate construction of a trans-Canada highway which will give work to thousands and thousands of people,' 'a St. Lawrence waterway which will take care of our farm and manufactured products' and then we shall give him a good rubbing with the famous salve called 'protection', the great panacea which has been advocated for so many years."

speechtext:
In rising to make my first speech in this house I am perhaps in the mental state of Macbeth, as described by Master William Shakespeare when he said:
My functions are smothered in surmise, and nothing is but what is not.
The House of Commons, Mr. Speaker, is a strange place to a new member, and although it is called parliament it is perhaps the last place in which a new member, even if he be a lawyer, desires to speak. I spoke to the hon. member for Mount Royal (Mr. White) before the house met this afternoon and he advised me that whatever I had to say perhaps I had better first try it out on the dog; but as I have no dog I am sorry to say that I shall have to try it out in the first instance and inflict it upon this parliament.
It is a very strange thing indeed for me to be here this evening. It is rather in the nature of a prophecy and also rather in the nature of the 'realization of a dream. Perhaps I shall discover it is a nightmare. But about sixteen years ago there was a young friend who, with myself, was preparing to go overseas. We came up to this hill one evening about 1915 when parliament was in memorable session. We stood overlooking the Ottawa river, and my friend, who is no longer here, turned to me and said: "You know, I have often dreamed that some day I shall be here in parliament. I don't know that I shall ever realize that dream, but if I am not here perhaps you will be." Mr. Speaker, it is one of the mysteries of mysteries that my friend, William George McIntyre, now lies asleep on Vimy Ridge, while I am here speaking in his place and, I hope, in the same spirit in which he spoke when he thus addressed me some sixteen years ago. I have wondered, especially since coming here, just what was in my friend's mind. I believe it was this: I believe he felt, as we all did

The Address-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
in those days, that the unity of our country was the great thing; not only the unity of our country but the unity of the world. It was that principle for which we fought, and it is that principle for which I trust I am here now.
Reflecting on that sentiment, I am prompted to make a protest. I desire here and now, as a young member, to protest against the kind of utterances that were made prior to the last election by certain hon. members then supporting the Liberal party. I refer by name to the Hon. Senator Lemieux, the Hon. Senator Casgrain and the Hon. Senator Dan-durand. I say that I believe it becomes me to protest on this occasion against the utterances which were made by these gentlemen just prior to July 28 last when, in the frenzy of fear lest they be driven from power, they tried to divide Canada again, in spite of the principles of unity which they had advocated at other times and which they should have advocated then. I did intend, Mr. Speaker, to bring their words here before parliament, to register them here in the records of this house, and protest against this sort of language as the kind of thing that ought not to be in this country. But I do not believe they deserve that much notice. I think, it would be far better for us and all Canada to remember the words and the work of Thomas d'Arcy McGee, the great patriot orator and martyr of confederation. Perhaps I can indicate to the house better what I mean if I quote what Thomas d'Arcy McGee said in 1861:
We Irishmen, Protestants and Catholics alike, born in a land of religious controversy, should never forget that we now live and act in a land of the fullest religious and civil liberty. All we have to do is each for himself, to keep down dissensions, which can only weaken, impoverish and keep back the country; each for himself to do all he can to increase its strength, its wealth and its reputation; each for himself, you and you gentlemen, and all of us, to welcome every talent, to take every invention, to cherish every gem of art, to foster every gleam of authorship, to honour every acquirement and every natural gift, to lift ourselves to the level of our destinies, to rise above all low limitations and narrow circumscriptions, to cultivate that, true catholicity of spirit which embraces all creeds, all classes and all races, in order to make our boundless province, so rich in known and unknown resources, a great, new northern nation.
When I quote the words of Thomas d'Arcy McGee I cannot help reflecting and wondering why he who was once the hon. Speaker of this house should forget that spirit and should propagate in the province of Quebec words animated and conceived against that very spirit.
There is an incident which Mr. McGee quotes in his confederation addresses, where he speaks about the establishment of the first Protestant church in Montreal. He said that .about the year 1790 the Presbyterians, both Canadian and American, organized themselves into a religious community in Montreal. They had no church, but they were given quarters by the Recollet Fathers there. Just imagine, Mr. Speaker, a situation like that, a situation where the disciples of John Knox were given by the Recollet Fathers in Montreal quarters wherein to carry out their religious observances. There was recorded in the minutes of that first Presbyterian organization their thanks to the Recollet Fathers, and it is recorded that they presented them with fifty-six .pounds of wax tapers and one hogshead of wine as a thank offering for what they had done for the First Presbyterian communion in Montreal. Thomas d'Arcy McGee in speaking of that said:
Gentlemen. I think this is an incident which could not be recorded and is perhaps not recorded in the annals of any other country.
I stand here a supporter of the Conservative party in this house and I am pleased and gratified beyond expression that we have supporting this government so many hon. members from the old province of Quebec. I am unable to speak their beautiful language; but I say to them as a British Canadian that I am glad they are here; I am glad that the long night is over and that the harvest has come to those who have stood for Canadian unity and for a union of the two races. Not only am I pleased, but I know the country is pleased and I believe it is a great thing for Canada.
If Your Honour will permit me, I desire to comment on the remarks of the right hon. gentleman, the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). In the great oration which he delivered he seemed to have the fervour of Edmund Burke, but I believe he had also the satire of Sheridan. The right hon. gentleman spoke for four and a half hours, and it is remarkable to me, representing as I do the constituency of Selkirk, when I recall that the communist candidate in that riding also spoke for four and a half hours. I believe he was just about as successful as was the right hon. gentleman in his diatribe against the Prime Minister. I do not believe it to be incumbent upon me, nor should I deem it wise, to analyze too freely or too carelessly some of the utterances made by the right hon. gentleman, but there is one in particular to which I desire to make reference.

The Address-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
I believe he was quoting the words of Sheridan when he said:
"I think, father," said he, "that many men who are called great patriots in the House of Commons, are great humbugs."
Perhaps it would be invidious for me to analyze that statement or to ask this house if it believed that there is any hon. member here who is a humbug, or if it is quite sure who are the patriots.

speechtext:
Patriotism always
means sacrifice, and I make that statement in spite of the laughter of the hon. gentlemen from Manitoba. I repeat again, patriotism entails sacrifice, but I do not know that the right hon. gentleman who used that term has made that sacrifice usually coupled with patriotism.	.
The implication contained in the remarks of the right hon. gentleman were nothing more than this: that the Prime Minister and leader of this house made proposals at the recent Imperial conference which were humbug.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext: Hear, hear.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ADDRESS IN REPLY
speechtext:
If my wits do not leave me altogether, I believe before I have finished that I will be able to prove that that term has boomeranged back to the leader of the opposition. I believe it will be made plain to everybody that the man who introduced that word in this house was himself the humbug.
With Your Honour's permission I would like to quote from an article by Mr. John L. Garvin, which appeared in the London Observer of -October 12, 1930. Speaking of the Imperial conference, Mr. Garvin said:
,, ()n. Wednesday the conference assembled at the foreign office to get down to business. The overseas statesmen spoke with the unprecedented frankness required at this juncture. Une and all they explained the only policy that can be useful to them and to us-extended preference for British manufacturers in their markets and broad reciprocal preference for dominion staples in ours. Other methods may be supplementary but they must be subsidiary. Nothing but preference all round can establish a ioundation for the closer economic cooperation of the empire.
Will hon. members please note these words: Mr. R. B. Bennett for Canada led the line.
Then all the other prime ministers of the self-governing dominions were behind him. I would much rather take the word of Mr. John L. Garvin, the greatest living journalist, than I would the word of the right hon. gentleman opposite. In the issue of the Observer of the following week, Mr. Garvin says:
(Mr. J. H. Stitt.]
The Daily Herald's proclamation does not mean the cabinet's no to Canada, it means the government's no to all the dominions. It is the dead hand of the old doctrinaire Liberalism laid upon the life of the empire and upon all that is fresh and growing and creative in the life of labour. Mr. Bennett of Canada is a Conservative appealing for change; Mr. Scullin, the Australian premier, is as good a labour man as any of them. Every child knew that reciprocal preference for Dominion staples in the mother country and for British manufacturers overseas, would be the fundamental proposition of the conference.
Will hon. gentlemen opposite please note the words:
The Daily Herald's proclamation does not mean the cabinet's no to Canada, it means the government's no to all the dominions.
There was a time in the history of' this country when Canadians led the line. As one of those Canadians who had a humble task in the line, I am happy to state that I followed the right hon. the Prime Minister and he certainly led the line and showed that Canada was the foremost of the overseas self-governing dominions.
Who was it used the word "humbug" in the first instance? If he will listen to me, I will direct my remarks to the right hon. the leader of the opposition. I believe it was Mr. Thomas, the Secretary of State for the Colonies, who used this word, and I would ask to be permitted to quote from pages 30 and 31 of the Journal of the Parliaments of the Empire. The following are in part the words of Mr. Thomas:
T ou do not render them a service by running away from the facts. They-
Speaking of the dominion prime ministers- -are prepared as we are prepared, to face them. They value these things and say so, but they much prefer to face the facts. We do not discuss these matters with them as partisans. Mr. Bennett did not come here as a Tory leader. Mr. Forbes did not come as a Liberal leader. Mr. Scullin did not come as a Labour leader. They all came as representatives of the dominions prepared to subordinate their particular party advantage and to examine the whole thing in the light of what is best for all.
Would you please note these words, which are those of Mr. Thomas:
The idea that they went away bitterly disappointed only exists in the minds of those who know nothing about the matter.
I believe that is almost sufficient criticism of the diatribe that was offered against the Prime Minister. Mr. Thomas continues:
It is not true, and I still say that whenever it opens, the Ottawa conference will have the benefit of the examination of a hundred and one matters which will be to the advantage of all concerned. We have said that we will go there free to examine every proposal on its

The Address-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
merits and not blindly say we accept it before we know what it is. That is not the way to run a government.
The best evidence that we have is that of Mr. Thomas himself who compliments the overseas prime ministers upon the manner in which they presented their case. If the attitude of the Prime Minister and his supporters at the Imperial conference was one really inimical to the welfare of the empire, and if hon. gentlemen opposite are real patriots, if they really have at heart the welfare of the empire, would they stand there hour after hour and day after day trying to engender in the minds of the people of Canada and possibly in the minds of the statesmen overseas the idea that the action of our representatives there was inimical to the welfare of the empire? Is that conceivable? It is not logical. The Prime Minister's admirable defence has been heard by all in this house. May I refer again to the words of Mr. Jebb, the historian of the Imperial conference, who said that the policy of the present Prime Minister was practically the same as that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. I notice that hon. gentlemen opposite took umbrage at that statement. The ex-Minister of .National Defence (Mr. Ralston) devoted almost his entire speech to an effort to explain to the house that the policy of the present Prime Minister was not that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, but I refer the house particularly to the words of the hon. member for Labelle (Mr. Bourassa). I believe he knows something about imperial affairs. What were his words? As reported at page 87 cf this year's Hansard, the hon. member for Labelle said that the Prime Minister was right when he said that he practically imitated the policy of Sir Wilfrid Laurier. Does that not reduce the whole argument of hon. gentlemen opposite to an absurdity? If what the Prime Minister proposed was humbug, then if Mr. Scullin and the other prime ministers stood behind our leader they were all humbugs, and if, as the hon. member for Labelle says, the Prime Minister's policy was practically an imitation of that of Sir Wilfrid Laurier, we have this unwitting Comment of the present leader of the Liberal party in this house, that Sir Wilfrid Laurier's proposals were humbug. That is analyzing logically the attitude of the right hon. the leader of the opposition.
When one considers the argument presented by the leader of the opposition, it. is best described by a story told by Mr. Peter McArthur some years ago in Toronto. When I heard this lengthy speech of the ex-Prime Minister I said to myself: It must be a phenomenon; it is absolutely phenomenal, with the country in the state in which it is,
that a man charged with the responsibility of leading His Majesty's loyal opposition should stand up for four and a half hours in the house and criticize, criticize, criticize, the policy of the Prime Minister, and notwithstanding the extremity in which we find ourselves, offer practically no remedy for the solution of our ills. Let me give the house the story of Peter McArthur. He was a good Liberal, and he was relating the story of a coloured preacher who was fond of using the word "phenomenon." After he had preached a rather lengthy discourse, he was proceeding home with one of his parishioners, and he said to his parishioner, "Did you notice the use of the word phenomenon?" The parishioner replied, "I sure did, but I do not know what it means." The preacher said, "I will tell you what it means." He put his hand into his pocket, and took out a nickel, saying, "That nickel is not a phenomenon." He pointed to a cow in the field and he said, "That cow is not a phenomenon." He also pointed to a thistle and he said, "That thistle is not a phenomenon. Do you hear that lark singing? That is not a phenomenon. But if that cow should try to chew the cud on that nickel and sit down on that thistle and then try to sing like a lark, it would be a phenomenon." It occurs to me that that definition of the word "phenomenon" accurately describes the attitude of the leader of the opposition towards the Prime Minister in his work at the Imperial conference.
I heard the wards of the ex-Minister of Justice (Mr. Lapointe) when he almost shed teal's over the British Empire. I believe he said in effect that the British Empire was a soul, a spirit, and he practically wept tears over it. I could not help thinking that if the right hon. gentleman's leader had been in his true preelection frame of mind he would have stood up, taken his pocket handkerchief from his coat-tail, wiped the tears from his face and said, "Me, too, I stand first for the British Empire." Then, perhaps, in order that the right hon. gentleman and the ex-Minister of Justice might be consoled, I thought in imagination possibly the hon. member for Vancouver Centre (Mr. Mackenzie) would rise in his best sepulchral manner, hold his hands over the two distressed hon. gentlemen weeping for the British Empire, and say, "Hush ye, hush ye, little pet ye, or the Black Douglas, he will get ye."
It seems to me that some of the addresses which have been presented to the house are very much like the bushel of chaff that contained a couple of grains of wheat which, after you searched for them through the bushel of chaff and found them, were not

The Address-Mr. Stitt (Selkirk)
worth the finding; they were full of sound and fury, signifying nothing. Perhaps one of the most remarkable spectacles that we have had in the house was the leader of the opposition working up his eloquence in his apostrophe to freedom in support of his friend the hon. member for Weyburn (Mr. Young) who, I believe, is now famous in the house for his pair of white socks. Sometimes it occurs to me that I can express myself a little better in rhyme than in prose. I thought that the right hon. gentleman and the hon. member for Weyburn were on a rocky shore with tall cat-tails growing round and the evening falling about them. These would probably be the appropriate words of the right hon. gentleman in his apostrophe to freedom-and hon. members must realize of course that the hon. member for Weyburn would be there acting as flag boy with the right hon. gentleman:
0	Freedom, sweet Freedom, we weep dear for thee,
We're driven, marooned on the Loyalist rocks,
We fly in high heaven our flag dear for thee,
How bravely it floats-'tis a white pair of socks.

I want to say that I am here to support the government. I am pleased to be in a position to support it and to be a follower of a man of the calibre and character of the right hon. gentleman who went over to England and led the line. In the words of General Jan Smuts, "Humanity has struck its tents and it is on the march." If we are to solve the problems of this country, if we are not to have to scrap all our forms of democracy, call them Liberalism or Pro-gressivism, or whatever you like; if we are to overcome our difficulties we must realize that humanity has struck its tents and that we are on the march. I say, Mr. Speaker, that it is impossible for me to answer the letters of my constituents clamouring for work. In the course of his speech, the right hon. leader of the opposition, pointed his finger at the Prime Minister and said:	"Remember how we
handled the affairs of the country, remember how we balanced all our budgets out of taxation. Don't you dare do anything else, don't you try to solve the problem now confronting the Dominion by means of a capital loan." I say to the right hon. leader of the opposition that that is the dead hand of laissez-faire Liberalism, and if the Prime Minister of this country is to be guided by it I do not believe that our problems will be salved. I speak as an honest man. I hoped if I had time, to plead the cause of agriculture and labour as reflected in my constituency.
