Mr. Speaker, last July, in the middle of a year of commercial and financial distress and of worldwide political upheaval, the King government appealed to the people. It was of course defeated. The Conservative party won success by insisting that its chief, now the Prime
o58	COMMONS
The Address-Mr. Mercier (St. Henri)
Minister, had a cure for unemployment, that he had a stimulant for the restoration of industry, and that his agricultural policy would enrich the wheat producers and the farmers to the extent of making them millionaires.
Eight months have gone by. Has unemployment been cured, or has it reached its maximum? No. In Canada, as in the countries of Europe, the year 1931 presses forward with its train of financial and political difficulties, and harassed by storms. Everywhere the number of unemployed is increasing; in Great Britain, in Germany, in Italy, in Belgium, in Holland, in Czechoslovakia, in Poland, in the United States, in Australia; and even in Canada, under a Conservative government that promised so much, our unemployed still represent about 25 per cent of the membership of the labour unions. Is it not true that agriculture is in a precarious condition, and that manufacturing industry also is endangered by the fall of prices? At this very moment the Canadian farmer is obliged to sacrifice his commodities at prices ridiculously low, so low as not to meet the cost of production. What will become of him? Where do the Bennett government and its supporters stand with their promises to help agriculture, to bring it back to a degree of prosperity even greater than that which it enjoyed under the Liberal government from 1922 until the sad hours of the worldwide economic crisis of 1930? What is the farmer going to do next summer to meet his farming expenses? He finds it hard to get the kind of labour necessary to carry on his farm, and by that time, without foreign markets in prospect in which to sell his crops, and with his local market crowded, he will be in an even more desperate condition than he is at the present time?
And what about our manufacturing industries? Is not the manufacturer to-day sacrificing his surplus stocks on the home market, stocks which he has been holding in his warehouse for a better price? For the past two months he has been throwing his goods on the domestic market at a constantly receding price. Everything is being sold at a sacrifice. As a consequence our industrial plants are not working full time. The budget soon to be brought down will enable us to judge whether the government null be able to give to Canada that era of prosperity promised by the right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Bennett) and his supporters during the recent campaign. We very much doubt if that promise will be redeemed. Certainly within the next month we shall be given the opportunity of discussing our friend's budget innovation, called high protection. I am one of those who believe that Canada, from a moral, [Mr. P. Mercier.l
social and commercial point of view, should be part of the whole civilized world; our country should follow the wude road travelled by humanity, and not isolate itself; we should cooperate with the nations of the world in a spirit of good wall; we should obtain commercial exchange of products in order to revive our export trade which shows a constant decrease. As proof of this may I quote the latest official figures of the National Revenue department. These figures constitute a barometer of our commercial condition:

What will be the net decrease for the past month? Our two railways and our maritime transport companies	are	looking for	morebusiness, which is absolutely needed. Our government	railway	and	merchant marine
showed a total deficit of $13,694,008.93 at the end of their last fiscal year.
Hon. gentlemen opposite contend that prosperity is coming back. I see it in their speeches, Mr. Speaker, but it is in no way an accomplished fact nor is there any likelihood of that statement becoming true for some time. Are not the incomes of our professional and business men decreasing? Have not the stock exchanges in Canada been visited by violent declines and real hurricanes which have taken away, piece by piece, the fortunes of the rich, the savings of the professional and business men and even the savings of the imprudent workingmen. The Prime Minister has announced through the press of this country that this year, under his administration, Canada will have a deficit of $100,000,000. With a policy of protection and isolation, Canada, an industrial and farming nation, now enters into a period of budget deficits, unfortunately, to roplace the surpluses of the King government from 1924 to 1930. When the Liberal party relinquished power in 1930 the government showed a surplus over all expenditures of $44,506,000. During that period of Liberal administration there was also a reduction of the colossal debt contracted by the Conservative party from September, 1911, to December, 1921, so surely it is time to say:
Is it not evident that, at times, false doctrines appear to be true?
On reading the newspapers, or European, Canadian and American reviews we see that the anxious world has turned its eyes towards

The Address-Mr. Harris
New York and that land of high protection, the United States. Even with the high tariff protection existing in that country, the condition of the United States has become worse Bankruptcies have increased by 46 per cent; iron production has decreased by 37 per cent ; steel production has also decreased by 35 per cent; the consumption of cotton has declined by 37 per cent and salaries have been decreased by 28 per cent. These are the consequences to-day of that high United States tariff protection. What are we to think of the future of our Dominion now that we are to have a similar protective policy which will be applied by the present government, after the experience at the special session of last September? The Canadian people will have the opportunity to pronounce themselves again and will find the proper remedy. Then the Liberal party will receive the justice it deserves, and which it did not receive in 1930 because the people were deceived.
The people of Canada are now asking the Bennett government to end unemployment as the Prime Minister and his elected candidates promised to do, because unemployment is financially ruining Canada as a whole as well as the individual provinces and municipalities, which are obliged to help the unemployed. The Prime Minister, who is also Minister of Finance, has answered and will answer agais with an increased tariff. He administers a non-patent medicine which is being used at this time by almost all countries. I refer to increased duties, the closure of our border lines to individuals and to merchandise, the laws against dumping and the artificial increase in prices, which is a temporary source of greater profits. These expedients are only attempts to cast off on someone else the weight of the evil which affects Canada as well as the other peoples of the world All the nations are using these expedients at the same time. They have not been useful to any nation, and the situation will be the same in Canada. Increased duties will be of no avail; at the most they will bring about an artificial prosperity -which will last only for a few months. Time will soon tell.
Canada, with a higher tariff, inaugurated at the session last September, is isolating itself. We are witnessing the disappearance of the equilibrium between production and consumption. That can mean only failure. The Liberal party believes in the bringing together of Canada and the other nations of the world; a policy of cooperation must prevail. May I quote, in the French language, the appropriate words of a well known economist, Mr. Guglielmo Ferrero:
II est Evident qu'aueun peuple ne pourra a lui seul, en s'isolant, retablir l'equilibre entre la production et la consommation. C'est encore un probleme universel. Les cinq continents souf-frent d'une maladie commune, et ils ne gueri-ront qu'ensemble. Nous vivons dans une epoque ou la misere et la prosperity font avalanche. Le probleme economique n'est pas d'ailleurs iso-le; il est. lui aussi, lie etroitement a la paix.
Detruit violemment par la guerre, l'equilibre entre la production et la consommation ne pourra se retablir serieusement qu'a la suite d'une longue periode de paix. Or la paix est aujour-d'hui le plus universel des problemes.
In conclusion, Mr. Speaker, I leave to the right hon. Prime Minister for study and consideration some verses by Sully Prud'homme, a great French poet, which would seem to apply now. I will read them, as they were written, in the French language:
Yiens! ne marche pas seul dans un jaloux sentier;
Mais suis les grands chemins que Fhumanite foule;
Les hommes ne sont forts, bons, et justes qu'en foule.
Ils s'achevent ensemble, aueun d'eux n'est entier.

Mr. Speaker, it is with great pleasure that I congratulate you on your elevation to your new position as first commoner among us. For some nine years I have had the privilege of being associated with you, sir, and during that time, in common with other members of this house, I have learned to love and admire not only you but the good lady who is so much thought of by members on all sides of this house. Your legal attainments, your soldierly bearing and your friendliness in days gone by to those of us who were somewhat younger, will not be forgotten, and our fondest hope is that you may be spared for many years to serve us in your present capacity.
With regard to the mover and the seconder of the address my position is rather unique. For four years I had the pleasure of sitting in this chamber with the member for North Grey who represented that constituency before the election of the young man who now occupies that position. I learned a great deal about North Grey; I had the privilege of speaking there on several occasions and of mixing with the people, and I came to know the hon. member (Mr. Porteous) long before he entered parliament. I say, sir, that we are happy to have him with us, and as one year succeeds another he will prove to be a valuable acquisition to this chamber.
In like manner, for some years I had the pleasure of being a seatmate of Mr. Doucet, a man from the land of Evangeline, from
The Address-Mr. Harris

which we now have the present member for Restigouche-Madawaska (Mr. Cormier). I learned at that time, sir, that what we had read of the great Canadians coming from that district was true, and I say to hon. members of this chamber and to you, Mr. Speaker, that what we have heard so far merely presages what we will hear in the future from the hon. member, whom I congratulate on the message which already he has left with us.
It would be nice to go on in this manner for some time, Mr. Speaker. Perhaps I might congratulate the right hon. leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) on the four and a half hour marathon speech which he delivered, and so on. But unfortunately the rules of the house restrict us to forty minutes, and if I might make a suggestion to the government in this regard it would be that on the clerk's table there might be a clock, divided into forty segments, so that those who have a peroration could time themselves and get it off their minds before the expiration of their time. I felt sorry the other day for the hon. member for West Edmonton (Mr. Stewart). He took over forty minutes and said little, and he found he did not have time for his peroration. We waited for it, and the probability is that in it he might have had something real to say.
One or two other members who have participated in the debate, are really the cause of my now saying a word or two. I would ask that the hon. member for North Wellington (Mr. Blair) be paged, because I am going to say something in reply to him, inasmuch as he made a reference to Toronto. The hon. member for Toronto West Centre (Mr. Factor) is not in the chamber; I should like to see him too. And the hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) also had something to say about Toronto; I should be glad to have him paged. But while we are waiting for these hon. gentlemen I might say a word or two in reference to the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King) and what he had to advance in the interests of the country in this debate.
A good deal has been said about the days of prosperity during the regime of the government he led; a good deal has been said by the leader of the opposition about deficits and so forth. Let me ask this house one question:	On whose budget has this country
been operating up to September of the fiscal year just closed? Was it the May day budget that laid dow'n the system of taxation from which revenues were going to be derived-revenues which were to take care of the run-

ning expenses of the country? Whose is the responsibility in this regard? Taxation measures should have been in the May day budget. I say to the leader of the opposition that we have not had a real budget in this house since the days of the late Mr. Fielding. The budget we had on May day last year was purely and simply a political budget. There was in it no estimate of the proposed expenditures or the proposed revenues, and this country found itself operating under that budget and heading for a deficit from the very day it came down in this chamber. And no one knows that better than does the leader of the opposition. He gave us statistics, lots of statistics; and he ended up his period at a very convenient point for himself, namely, the end of the fiscal year, March 31, 1930. But he had in his possession the figures up to the end of February of this year. If he did not want to use them why was he not fair, not only to his own members but to Canada, and give the figures he had at least until the end of July? Why stop a year ago? The leader of the opposition said, as reported at page 18 of Hansard:
In short, a condition exists in this country at the moment the like of which, fortunately, it has not witnessed at any time heretofore in her history.
He was asked when he first noticed it, and he replied:
It has been noticed by everyone since this administration came into office.
He knows in his heart that this is not a fair statement. He knows that these conditions were brought about to a large degree by a world situation. If he does not, let me refer him to some of the statements of his own followers. The hon. member for Last Mountain (Mr. Butcher) says, as reported at page 236 of Hansard:
I frankly and freely admit that the Conservative party in power to-day is not and cannot be held wholly responsible for the unhappy conditions that exist at the present time both in the matter of the lack of market for our farm products and in the matter of unemployment.
And the hon. member for Toronto West Centre 'had this to say:
Whatever unemployment, whatever suffering exists in this country was due to world conditions. . . .
The hon. member for Red Deer (Mr. Speakman) also had something to say. We are glad to see him back in the chamber again, restored to his usual health and vigour. He is reported:
I have been asked many a time, is it the fault of the present government. Well, Air. Speaker, to be perfectly frank I will say, no, in the

The Address-Mr. Harris
main it is not. . . . They have been in power only a few months and they had neither the time nor the opportunity to go into the present situation in any large way.
These are the statements of hon. gentlemen surrounding the leader of the opposition, and he knew better than to make the statements he did make. World depression is with us; we all admit that. It is a cycle and seems to come after great world events. Go back to the days of a hundred and fifty years ago in the time of the Napoleonic wars and you will find the fact illustrated graphically in Goldman's Graphic Charts giving statistics with regard to world conditions. The year 1790 is used as the base in connection with wholesale commodity prices of all sorts of goods on the London auctions. The Napoleonic wars came on two years later, but using 1790 as the base, with the figure 100, we find that in 1800, after eight years of war, it had risen to 175. By 1809 it was 195 and by 1830, at the conclusion of the wars, it recedes again to 100, and lies along the base of 100 for some years until the advent of the Civil war, 1861-65, when it again moves from the figure 100 to as high as 215, receding again in 1875 to 100, and remaining pretty well on that base-a a little below at times, and occasionally a little above it-until 1912, when it moves to 110, and we find that with the advent of the great world war the wholesale commodity prices again reach the figure 215. And now they are receding.
These charts show that the same state of affairs has prevailed in each of these three periods, with this difference, that to-day we have the advantage of more than 100 years of modern civilization. We must be guided very carefully in getting back to pre-war conditions, and it is the duty of the government to see to it that they are so guided. We have a condition of cartels in the eastern hemisphere of Europe and Great Britain, in the lines of nearly all manufactured goods, these countries dumping their surplus on communities such as this. We have a condition of trusts in that gigantic nation to the south of us, which have a tendency to hold up the prices of nationally advertised goods and to control them. These conditions make it difficult for us to recede to the position to which we shall have to get back, which is something similar to pre-war conditions. Our people themselves, we find, are accustomed to the new luxuries they have had and will be slow to give them up. But little by little we shall have to get back to that pre-war state.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre (Mr. Woodsworth) a few days ago gave us a chart showing that products had receded in the agricultural line much faster than in other 22110-36
lines. It is true that agriculture is one of the first industries to suffer in our economic system; and when it does, the effect, seems to permeate the whole country, bringing distress with it. But fortunately in this country the people of strongest fibre are to be found among the agriculturists, and you will find them to-day getting ready to put in their crops once more as they have done in years gone by. And with the fortitude and courage characteristic of them, assured that this country is guided by a strong government such as we have to-day, Canada, as no other country can, will come through this depression. Throughout my entire remarks, if I cannot do anything else, I wish to leave this one impression, that this Canada of ours is a grand and glorious place to live in, and I am very optimistic with regard to the future.
The hon. member for Winnipeg North Centre, in the chart to which I have referred, showed that western grain prices had receded 59 per cent while the price of farm products had gone down 34 per cent. The right hon. leader of the opposition gave us figures with regard .to our export trade and he would lead this country to believe that all our export trade is demoralized. Might I bring to the attention of this house the fact that Canada is still doing a very large volume of export trade and will continue to do so. I am sorry the hon. member for Toronto West Centre is not in his seat because I believe a reply should be made to the statements he gave to this house. He complained about the unemployment situation and stated that it had not been relieved to the degree to which he would like to see it relieved. On page 309 of Hansard he says:
In the latest official information furnished the press on March 11 we find that 228,351 individuals have been given employment and 3,975,355 man-days have been afforded to them from the commencement of operations under the Unemployment Eelief Act up to February 28, 1931.
The hon. member stated that unemployment was just as acute as it ever has been, if not in fact, worse. The hon. member who has just taken his seat made a similar statement and said that it was still down 25 per cent, or some such figure. My answer to the hon! members who sit behind the leader of the opposition is this: where would this country have been, how much more acute would have been the situation, had the people through a mistake put into power last july the "not a nickel" government? We know that the people realized that what was needed in -Canada at that time was a man at the head of our democracy who would give action instead of platitudes, who would give work instead of statistics and who would give real leadership instead of imbecility and non-leadership.
The right hon. leader of the opposition had something to say in this regard, and in reply I would say that I was reminded of his stand while trying to put the children to bed after church on Sunday evening. We were singing that little nursery rhyme, "Ding Dong Bell, Pussy's in the Well," but I would like to change that to:
Ding dong bell, Canada's in the well.
Who put her in? Little Willie King.
WTe might go a little further and say:
Who'll pull her out? E. B. Bennett, no doubt.
The right hon. gentleman complains bitterly that we are not making haste. He wants to know where is the national highway, or what progress is being made with the St. Lawrence
(Mr. Harris.]
development. He did not think so much about that, during the nine years he was in power. He asked: Where is the aid to agriculture, technical education, old age pensions and so on? Little by little these things are coming.
The hon. member for Charlevoix-Saguenay (Mr. Casgrain) made an interesting contribution to this debate the other day. He mentioned the city of Toronto and said he re-jretted that one hundred mechanics, carpenters, bricklayers, technicians and contractors had been guaranteed employment in soviet Russia. Arrangements for their sailing had been made, this party being composed of Russians, Canadians, Frenchmen, Finlanders and others-one hundred men out of a population of 600,000. It might be just as well for Canada if a few more people possessing the idea that civilization would be best benefited by the ideals worked into the fabric of the present Russian constitution would take a trip abroad and stay there. Perhaps we could suggest a few hon. members from the other side who might go along. I hesitate to suggest that the hon. member for Southeast Grey (Miss Macphail) might even go as a chaperone. Then, in order to make sure that he would be right with his own constituency, the hon. member said: Most of us in the province of Quebec felt as proud as did the Prime Minister when he heard that he was breaking off trade negotiations with Russia. Consistency, thou art a virtue, but where is the virtue in that statement of the hon. member? Then the same hon. gentleman-I do not seem to be able to get his attention-said: We ought to have some real economy in this government, we should get rid of some of these 'departments, the Department of the Interior, for instance. He did not think of that when the natural resources were being turned back while his old administration was in power. He did not think of that when the charwomen were drawing their last pay envelopes. The hon. member-he still will not give me any attention-went on to say that we were going to have a new tariff board.

We have his attention now. We have also the attention of the leader of the opposition (Mr. Mackenzie King). Among other things the right hon. gentleman had something to say about old age pensions. I was sorry to see a man of his calibre stoop to this method of insinuating in the way he did when, as is reported on page 21 of this year's Hansard, he made this statement in regard to old age pensions:
Every old man and old woman who had a vote was made to believe that he and she were going to get full pensions as soon as this parliament met, but now they are told that they will get it as soon as the current economic situation warrants.
Let me couple with him on that occasion the hon. member for North Wellington, who seems to know a good deal about old age pensions. In this regard I want to be kind to the honourable, ethical doctor. I am referring now to the speech he made away back last September. If he thought he was wrong, he had plenty of opportunity to square himself with the public. I waited, listened to another speech by him in the house, and still he did not correct himself. Therefore to-night I shall have something to say on the subject of his ideas on old age pensions. As reported at page 134 of Hansard of September, 1930, he said:
I do not think any persons in my district received an old age pension without being distinctly led to understand that they would lose it if they voted the wrong way.
This was playing on the feelings of those of our citizens who have given of their best to further the interests of Canada, many of them during the pioneer days in different parts of the country. This sort of appeal does not in my opinion find a response on the part of the real Canadian people. He was a new member, he used the privileges of the house and he had a score or more of editorials in his local press brought to his attention, giving him an opportunity to retract statements he had made. As reported oh page 133 of Hansard of last session, he said:
The widows' and orphans' fund was interfered with. I do not believe such statements were true, yet the influence came, as it were, from Toronto; that idea seemed to permeate the riding and it was very hard to offset it.
He said that when they wanted to get votes in North Wellington, they had to go out like Nicodemus in the dark, and try to secure them. Then he goes on to speak about the condition of the farmers. He also said:
In the district which I represent are a great many comparatively poor farmers. Many farms are being sold for tax purposes. The farmers are in extreme need.

The hon. gentleman, when he made these representations, was from one end of his constituency to the other the subject of editorials. The Palmerston Spectator bad this to say to him:	*
Doctor Blair, member of parliament for North Wellington, was telling the nrembers of the House of Commons that intimidation was practised in this riding during the recent election. We believe the electors of this riding have a right to a full knowledge of conditions as they actually exist and we believe it is up to Doctor Blair to fully explain his remarks in the house.
In the Fergus News-Record they say:
These charges are serious.

That in view of the alleged serious charges made by Doctor J. K. I say to the hon. member that he has privileges in the house, but those privileges are not here to be abused. He has the right when he makes reply to back up his statements with real facts. I rather thought he was going to do that a day or two ago when he again spoke in this chamber, but he followed the same line of attack as he had done before, offering no apology in the face of all these editorials. But something was forthcoming afterwards. It was a letter written to his constituents. I have a copy of it in my hand, and it is headed, "House of Commons, Ottawa, March 23, 1931," and addressed "Cheer up Henry." It reads:
The Address-Mr. Harris

Dear Sir:
We are having lovely weather here, and we sure are having a lively session. We are working real hard, and there is plenty of work to do, but I enjoy it very much.
I have a lot to learn. I have a considerable advantage over some because of my education. I do not require to have problems worked out for me that arise in mathematics, but in questions of opinions and logic the answer is not quite so plain as it is in arithmetic.
I spoke for 35 minutes the other day to the speech from the throne. I was requested to do so by the Hon. Mackenzie King, and after I had finished he came back and shook hands and congratulated me, remarking that I did real well, and that he saw in me some splendid timber for new debates, so that cheered up my drooping spirits, because I was not too well pleased with my own remarks. I tried to lay Mr. Bennett's promises before him regarding agriculture, and I appealed to him to help the farmers in whatever way he deemed best.
The room and crowd is so large here, it is not like speaking in Arthur, and it takes some nerve. Mr. Sinclair was here the fourth year before he gave his maiden speech. I am" too impetuous to remain that long, especially as I think the people are not getting a fair deal.
I will drop a line again later. Hoping you are all well, I am,
.	Yours truly,
Jno. K. Blair, M.P.
I rather apologize for occupying the time of the house with this particular matter, 'but statements of this kind, which have no 'basis in fact, should not be made in the house. A member should not exercise his privilege in the house in that way. When the bon. member says thait the former member did not speak in this chamber for four years, that is not a fact. The hon. member says that he is good at arithmetic, but his arithmetic is all wrong. The gentleman who formerly represented North Wellington took his seat on February 5, 1925, and- he. spoke, on a budget debate on March 6, 1928. Is that four fears? He raised a question in the house in 1927. Does twenty-five from twenty-seven leave four? He spoke in the committee on agriculture the first time he was on that committee. Is that four years? I say to the hon. member for North Wellington: Your arithmetic is wrong. You have got a very wrong conception of your duty in this house to your constituents. I say to the hon. member for North Wellington that he will learn before he is here very long that there is a time to speak and a time to bridle his tongue. You will learn that there is a time to give service to your constituents in committee as well as an opportunity to waste the time of this House of Commons. You will learn there are common decencies in vogue in this chamber; you will learn that your constituents expect nation-wide views as well as picayune local politics; you will learn we expect state-

meats backed by facts; you will learn that it is undesirable to inspire or inculcate into the minds of your constituents a distrust in democratic forms of government. You will learn that there are some ethics in politics as well as in the medical profession. You will learn, sir, that your wonderful educational attainments which were of such great advantage to you over other hon. members in this chamber are outweighed many many times by the small picayune frame of mind in which you address yourself to the problems which come for attention in this chamber.

My hon. friend from North Wellington will probably learn to accept congratulations in modesty from his leader. He will learn that perhaps the real timber is not all found in this chamber but that some is still in the maple bushes back in North Wellington. Concerning the hon. member who on a previous occasion occupied the seat of my hon. friend I doubt if there is one man who will rise in his place and say that that member was not the image of the best in Canada. Was he not the mirror of his own constituency? Was he not beloved by all members who sat on both sides of this house? To reflect on a former member is in rny humble judgment a misdemeanor for which the hon. member at present, representing the constituency of North Wellington will have ample opportunity of making amends; or, as his own newspapers ask him to do, he should either substantiate his statements or apologize for making them.
I am sorry, Mr. Speaker, to have trespassed on the time of the house so long in this regard. Let me say that so far as Canada as a whole is concerned this government is making lapid progress with its great task. Canada ds the only country in the empire, yea I believe in the civilized world, in which to-day industries have taken on new hands. Old factories are being renovated and enlarged; vacant buildings are being rehabilitated for new lines of production and enterprise. Our good farmers, even those in North Wellington who are so afraid of being sold for taxes, are planning to put jn as big a crop as they have done before. I would say- that sixty per cent are not worrying about this parliament and perhaps do not know that it is in session. They are plowing their furrows; they are hoeing their rows, and they have faith in the country which has done so much for them. There is in their breasts and in the breasts of all Canadians to a greater degree than in any other part of the civilized world

The Address-Mr. Dubois
a hope and courage that in that final analysis will weigh heavily in the economic plans of world affairs. We see to-day processions of new industries coming not only from the United States but from the mother country. Employment has been extended to a quarter of a million of wage earners. Sixty-five American manufacturers are establishing branches in the Dominion and many other negotiations are in progress. Time and again the statement is made that these industries are located here on account of the policy of the present administration. Canadians are returning from the republic to the south and side by side with them are others coming to this land of opportunity. Since the beginning of the economic depression the development of Canada has far surpassed that of any other country. We are seeing the beginning of greater things. Step by step we are fast getting out of the present depression and side by side with the mother country and other parts of the empire we are making real, genuine, sound progress. So long as this party is in power we will not only see the empire retain its place in the sun but we will see our glorious empire go on from point to point, as she has done in the last thousand years, continuing to be the greatest agency for good that civilization has ever known.
